docs.text: In *nix environments, the user dedicated to administering the operating system, with special privileges to install, configure and maintain the software. Other users can inherit those privileges if they belong to the root user group.

docs.title: LTS version
docs.text: Long-term support version. It is supported for two years, extendable by another two with a long-term support contract. It receives security and critical bug patches, not features from newer versions, and it coexists with Feature Releases, which bring the new features. See Version and support policy.

docs.title: Warp Update
docs.text: Update system from the console itself. Its wizards download, apply and verify the update, and there is also an offline mode for isolated environments. It is the recommended way as opposed to the manual update. See Updates.

docs.title: Watchdog
docs.text: Feature that checks whether a system is running and, if it is down, restarts it.

docs.title: Widget
docs.text: Interface element that provides a single point of interaction for a type of data. It shows a layout of the information that the user can modify, such as a window or a text box. Combined in an application, they hold the data processed by it and the interactions available on that data.

docs.title: 3. Compatibility and migration to the new server architecture
Compatibility and migration to the new server architecture
docs.text: Pandora Server gathers the specialised servers into a single multithreaded application: each one walks its own task queue (modules to process, agents to scan, alerts to evaluate) with its own number of threads. This annex describes how remote monitoring is shared out today and what is left of the previous generation of instances specialised by type of check. The number of processes in the system is not deduced from that split.

docs.title: Why fewer servers
docs.text:
The previous generation had more specialised instances: ICMP, SNMP, WMI, remote plugins and remote inventory, among others. The wiki describes a high memory footprint even before processing modules; it does not state that each subtype was an independent operating system process.

The change groups several types of check into the same server, with more threads inside. The network consumer can handle WMI and ICMP when networkhpserver is disabled, with no need for a specialised instance per type. Each check keeps its own timeout: grouping servers does not mean levelling their timeouts.

docs.title: Historical inventory of servers
docs.text:
The wiki lists 21 names from the previous generation. It is a historical inventory, not the list of servers the current configuration starts, nor a forecast of the ones that will exist in other versions:

Data Server · SNMP Console · Syslog Server · Export Server · Sync Server · Discovery Server · WEB Server · Network Server · WMI Server · Plugins Server · Inventory Server · ICMP Server · SNMP Server · Event Server · Log Server · SIEM Server · NetFlow Server (including sFlow) · NCM Server · Policy Manager Server · WUX Server · MADE Server.

In that list, SNMP Server meant SNMP module checks; SNMP Console received traps. The old names do not by themselves amount to specialised instances in the current start-up.

docs.title: What each server does today
docs.text:
Of the whole family of servers that existed, only three share out remote monitoring today (agents with no EndPoint, or EndPoints also checked from outside):

Server Token What it runs Network (Network Server) networkserver TCP, remote commands (SSH and Windows remote), WMI, prediction modules and web modules; also ordinary ICMP and SNMP if networkhpserver is explicitly disabled High-performance network (Network HP Server) networkhpserver ICMP in bulk with fping and SNMP in bulk with pandorafsnmp (v1, v2c and v3) Heavy (Heavy Server) heavyserver Remote server plugins, remote inventory, network device configuration management (NCM) and export of data to another Pandora FMS

The split of ICMP and SNMP between the first two is not a choice the administrator makes module by module: with the Network High Performance Server running (it comes that way from the factory), the Network Server gives up ICMP and SNMP and keeps the rest; if networkhpserver is explicitly disabled, the Network Server takes charge of both again, query by query, with the system tools instead of the bulk processing. There is only one exception: an SNMP module that builds up more errors than the retry allows (braa_retries) falls to the Network Server, even if the high-performance one is still running. If the high-performance server does not start for lack of fping or braa, its constructor does not disable networkhpserver: an automatic switch of ICMP and SNMP must not be taken for granted. The details of the split are in Network monitoring.

Two servers from the previous version's list disappeared without leaving a replacement of their own: the prediction server and the web server. Their functions were not taken over by a new server, but by the Network Server itself, which identifies the module type before running it and calls the prediction routine or the web check one as appropriate, without going through a different specialised instance.

Besides these three, the wiki describes servers tied to the master: the policy manager on a node, and migration and autoprovisioning on a Command Center. The policy manager is not a server of its own: it runs from the console itself, not as an independent server process. Migration and autoprovisioning in the Command Center do rely on a server switch of their own (see the provisioningserver token in the full reference). The synchronisation server is disabled from the factory; to start it requires syncserver enabled and sync_address set. Its constructor does not require it to be master.

docs.title: Servers enabled by default
docs.text:
The template enables five servers and leaves the eleven switches listed below disabled. The actual start-up also depends on the requirements of each component. These are template values, not the internal values the parser uses when an option is missing, nor an exhaustive inventory of every function in the product (see the full reference for each token):

Enabled in the template Disabled in the template Data (dataserver) SNMP console (snmpconsole) Network (networkserver) Events (eventserver) High-performance network (networkhpserver) Log (logserver) Heavy (heavyserver) WUX (wuxserver) Discovery (discoveryserver) Syslog (syslogserver) — RMM (rmmserver) — Alerts (alertserver) — NetFlow (netflowserver) — MADE (madeserver) — SIEM (siemserver) — SIEM events (siemevents)

The wiki's disabled list includes Mainframe Server, but there is no equivalent switch among the tokens of this template or among the options that Config.pm parses in the checkout examined. No default value is attributed to it for that reason, nor is it inferred that it does not exist in other components. The wiki described Export Server as disabled by default in the previous split; heavyserver 1 does not allow deducing the current state of the export.

docs.title: Retired tokens and their replacement
docs.text:
Installation from the server packages examined places the usual configuration at /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf. The executable accepts the path of the file as an argument, so that location is not mandatory in every installation. To change activation or threads, edit the file that your service uses.

The legacy switches are still read in pandora_server.conf, but they do not instantiate the old servers in the current start-up path. The old thread tokens are also parsed, but they do not adjust the threads of the servers that perform those tasks today: the new thread token given in each row has to be configured.

Legacy token (activation / threads) Current function Replacement for activation / threads predictionserver / prediction_threads Prediction networkserver / network_threads webserver / web_threads Web networkserver / network_threads wmiserver / wmi_threads WMI networkserver / network_threads icmpserver / icmp_threads ICMP networkhpserver / networkhpserver_threads; with HP disabled, networkserver / network_threads snmpserver / snmp_threads SNMP networkhpserver / networkhpserver_threads; with HP disabled or when braa_retries is exceeded, networkserver / network_threads pluginserver / plugin_threads Remote plugins heavyserver / heavyserver_threads inventoryserver / inventory_threads Remote inventory heavyserver / heavyserver_threads exportserver / export_threads Export heavyserver / heavyserver_threads ncmserver / ncmserver_threads NCM heavyserver / heavyserver_threads

snmpserver also keeps a specific read to check the activity of snmptrapd; it does not enable SNMP module processing.

reconserver and recon_threads are a different case, not a simple equivalence: a network reconnaissance server separate from Discovery never existed. reconserver is today a second power switch for the Discovery Server itself, an alternative to discoveryserver (it is enough for one of the two to be active), and recon_threads still has an effect: the number of threads Discovery uses is the higher of discovery_threads and recon_threads, not one of the two exclusively. It is better not to touch it blindly thinking that it is a leftover with no effect.

docs.title: Checks with short intervals
docs.text:
The usual check interval is 300 seconds (5 minutes). The module editor of the Web console allows intervals of 15 seconds for ICMP availability and latency and for numeric and incremental numeric SNMP; the editor rejects values below 15 seconds and corrects them with a warning. The same validation sets 300 seconds for asynchronous types 21, 22 and 23, and 60 seconds for the other checked types. It exempts Data Server modules before applying those minimums: it is not a universal prohibition for every module, nor does it prove an equivalent validation in the server.

The 300-second threshold also affects two other behaviours:

  • No unknown status is generated. The periodic check that marks a module as unknown when it has gone too long without data requires an interval of 300 seconds or more; with a shorter interval, that module does not move to unknown through that inactivity check.
  • Data precision changes: process_data formats numeric data with five decimals when module_interval is 300 seconds or less, and with one when it exceeds 300 seconds. The wiki describes the reverse order.

docs.title: Compaction and deletion of short-interval data
docs.text:
With an enabled and working connection to the historical database, maintenance calls pandora_historydb_smallint with a window of 7 days for modules with module_interval greater than zero and less than 300 seconds. The hook selects those modules and calls the transfer to the historical database per module. The purge and the general transfer run before, so those seven days do not guarantee a universal week of retention, nor the transfer when there is no connection to the historical database. It is not a window that can be configured from Performance.

The transfer of numeric data to the historical database may apply a compaction by time intervals; text data does not enter that branch. It is disabled from the factory (days_compact=0); step_compact is 1 sample per hour from the factory, not the five stated in the wiki. The Web console allows configuring it between 1 and 12; the routine also limits values outside that range. Compaction groups the numeric samples by module and interval: it calculates the mean or, for _proc types, keeps zero if any zero appears. It is not the same as promising an exact number of samples retained per hour in every case. The option lives in Settings → System Settings → Performance, next to the rest of the purges.

docs.title: 4. Extending the SNMP and WMI wizards with custom components
Extending the SNMP and WMI wizards with custom components
docs.text: The SNMP and WMI wizards of the agent view (see SNMP wizard and Windows without an agent: WMI) do not bring a fixed list of modules: they propose what they find in a catalogue of wizard components. This annex explains how to extend that catalogue with manufacturers and custom components, for both wizards.

docs.title: What wizard components are and when to create them
docs.text:
A wizard component is a template that describes what to query on the device and how to turn it into a module. When the wizard explores a device, it does not improvise: it walks this catalogue and offers the components that match what it has found (the manufacturer, in SNMP), grouped in blocks according to what they measure.

Creating a custom one is worth it in three cases: a manufacturer the wizard does not recognise yet (the "PEN is not registered" error of SNMP wizard), a proprietary OID that should always be at hand without looking it up every time, or a piece of data that does not come out of a single OID but of combining several. The difference from an ordinary network component is the origin: that one is applied by hand, choosing it in the module editor; a wizard component is proposed by the wizard after exploring the device, and a single one can end up generating many modules at once, one per row it finds.

When to create one and when not to

A switch the SNMP wizard already recognises, but which lacks a manufacturer's proprietary temperature sensor: no new component is needed, with SNMP modules and the OID at hand it is enough for that one-off case. If, on the other hand, the same temperature probe is going to be repeated across dozens of devices from the same manufacturer, a wizard component saves creating it by hand on each one.

docs.title: Registering a manufacturer (PEN)
docs.text:
The SNMP wizard identifies the manufacturer of the device by its PEN (Private Enterprise Number): a number that every manufacturer registers with IANA and that occupies a fixed position inside the sysObjectID the device declares. If Pandora FMS does not have that PEN registered, the wizard stops with the "PEN is not registered" warning and proposes no component, even if the device answers perfectly over SNMP.

Registering the PEN is the first step, in Management → Configuration → Templates → Private Enterprise Numbers, with three fields: PEN (the number the device declares), Manufacturer (the short name that later identifies its components) and Description. Registering the PEN only gives the manufacturer a name; it does not create a single module on its own, that is done by the components of the next section. It requires console management permission.

The installation brings 27 manufacturers already registered, but only some of them bring wizard components as well: Cisco, HP, Juniper, F5, Fortinet and two generic numbers for the devices that expose their information with Net-SNMP/UCD, to which the generic components (All) that are offered to any device are added. The rest of the manufacturers registered from the factory (D-Link, MikroTik, Alcatel-Lucent, Ubiquiti, Allied Telesis, IBM, Dell, Apple, Oracle, Hitachi, Synology, Fujitsu, among others) no longer make the wizard stop, but they only receive those generic components until custom components are created for them. A manufacturer that is not in the list has to be registered by hand, as in the following example.

Registering a UPS the wizard does not recognise

A UPS declares a PEN that is not in the factory catalogue. It is registered with its IANA number in PEN, my-ups in Manufacturer and a brief description. From then on the wizard no longer stops because of an unregistered PEN, although for the moment it proposes no module: that comes with the first component of the next section.

docs.title: Creating a wizard component
docs.text:
Wizard components are created in Management → Configuration → Templates → Remote components, choosing the wizard component type. They share with an ordinary network component the usual fields —enabled, Add by default (whether it appears already checked when the wizard opens), name, data type, component group (the block in which it appears grouped), unit and thresholds, description— plus the Module protocol (SNMP or WMI) and the Manufacturer ID: a specific manufacturer already registered, or All, which offers the component for any device regardless of its PEN.

Two fields decide the rest of the form and what kind of module the component is going to propose:

  • Scan Type: Fixed creates a single module; Dynamic walks a table of the device and creates one module per row it finds, without knowing in advance how many there are going to be.
  • Execution type: Network makes the server itself read the value directly, like a normal SNMP or WMI module; Plugin delegates the calculation to a server plugin or, if the wizard is launched from a satellite server, to a module_exec command.
Scan Execution What it creates Fixed Network A single module that reads an OID (or a WMI query) directly Fixed Plugin A single module whose value is calculated by a plugin, from one or several OIDs or fields Dynamic Network One module per row of a table, read directly Dynamic Plugin One module per row of a table, calculated by a plugin

Duplicating an existing component with the Duplicate action of its listing is the quickest starting point for a similar new one; there is no import or export of components between installations.

docs.title: SNMP components with a static OID
docs.text:
Fixed scan + network execution, the simplest combination: Value OID is the final OID that is going to be read, just as in an SNMP module created by hand. Name OID is optional and, if filled in, its value replaces the _nameOID_ macro in the module name.

Battery charge of a UPS

With the my-ups manufacturer already registered, a fixed component called "Battery charge" with the proprietary charge OID in Value OID, warning and critical thresholds already filled in and the "Power" component group. As soon as the SNMP wizard is launched on an agent of that manufacturer, the component appears in its corresponding block, ready to be checked.

docs.title: SNMP components with a dynamic OID
docs.text:
Dynamic scan + network execution: Value OID and Name OID stop being final OIDs and become two branches (subtrees) of the device. The wizard walks both of them completely, crosses the results by index —the same index in both branches corresponds to the same row— and proposes one module per index found, with the name of that row replacing _nameOID_ and the index itself appended to the end of Value OID.

One module per temperature sensor

A proprietary table exposes, for each temperature sensor of the device, its name in one branch and its value in another. A dynamic component with Name OID pointing to the branch of names and Value OID to the branch of values creates, after the exploration, one module per sensor found, each one with the real name of its sensor.

docs.title: SNMP components calculated by a plugin
docs.text:
For a piece of data that does not come out of reading a single OID, execution switches to Plugin. The form then adds four things:

  • Macros OID: one entry for each OID that takes part in the calculation, which is referenced in the rest of the form as _oid_1_, _oid_2_…
  • Value operation: the formula that combines those values, written with the same _oid_N_ macros. It only serves to show the value in the wizard preview; the module that is created does not use it.
  • Server plugin: the plugin that does the calculation for real every time the module runs. The two factory ones share the same connection fields (_address_, _port_, _version_, _community_ and the SNMPv3 credentials), but they differ in what they ask next:
    • Wizard SNMP module, for numeric values: besides the connection, it asks for the OID list (_oid_1_,_oid_2_…) and the Operation: the formula that combines those values written as _o1_, _o2_… according to the position of each OID in the list.
    • Wizard SNMP process, to know whether a process is running: instead of a list of OIDs, it asks for a single Process field with the name of the process (case sensitive); the plugin checks by itself, against the SNMP process tree of the system, whether it appears as running.
  • Satellite execution: the equivalent command for when the wizard is launched from a satellite server, which uses the wizard_snmp_module and wizard_snmp_process plugins installed on the satellite.

Since the preview and the real execution use different fields, the formula in Value operation and the one in Operation must say the same thing; if not, the wizard proposes one value and the module ends up measuring another.

In dynamic scan, each _oid_N_ stops being a final OID and becomes a branch that is also walked by index, just as in the previous section; the wizard calculates one value —and therefore one module— per row found.

Usage percentage of a partition

Two OIDs of a storage table, used space and total space, are registered in Macros OID as _oid_1_ and _oid_2_. Value operation is filled in with (_oid_1_ * 100) / _oid_2_, so that the preview already shows the percentage. In Server plugin, "Wizard SNMP module" is chosen, with _oid_1_,_oid_2_ in the OID list and (_o1_ * 100) / _o2_ in Operation; the connection fields are left with their macros. Each module created calculates the usage percentage on every run, with no post processing.

docs.title: WMI components
docs.text:
The WMI wizard uses the same component mechanism, with its own set of fields: WMI class (the class that is going to be queried), Query key field (which column of the response identifies each row) and Query extra fields (the rest of the columns that are needed). Each column is available as a _FIELDNAME_ macro with the value of that row. As in SNMP, dynamic means one module per row that the scan query returns.

The Query filters limit, on one hand, which rows the exploration returns and, on the other, how the value of the module is calculated in network execution:

  • Field value: the number of the column of the response whose value becomes the value of the module (0 is the key field itself; 1 onwards, each extra query field in its order).
  • Key string: optional. If filled in, the value of the module stops being the raw data and becomes 1 or 0 depending on whether it matches this string. This filter is not applied when the wizard is launched from a satellite server: the module generated on the satellite always returns the raw data of Field value, even if Key string has been filled in.

In plugin execution, instead of these two filters the following appear:

  • Value operation: the formula that combines the fields of the row with the _f1_, _f2_… macros (one for each extra query field, in order).
  • Server plugin: the plugin that does the calculation; the factory one is "Wizard WMI module", with the _class_wmi_ macro for the queried class and the same _f1_, _f2_… family in its Operation field.
  • Satellite execution: the equivalent command for when the wizard is launched from a satellite server, with the wizard_wmi_module plugin installed there.

Free space of each local disk

A dynamic WMI component on the Win32_LogicalDisk class, with the query filter DriveType = 3 (local disks only) and _DeviceID_ in the module name: the wizard creates, on each Windows device, one free space module for each local disk it finds, with the drive letter in the name itself.

docs.title: Field reference
docs.text: Field Protocol What it is for Add by default Common The component appears already checked when the wizard opens Component group Common Block in which the component is grouped inside the wizard Module protocol Common SNMP or WMI Manufacturer ID SNMP Manufacturer (registered PEN) the component is offered to, or All for any Scan Type Common Fixed (one module) or Dynamic (one module per row) Execution type Common Network (direct read) or Plugin (delegated calculation) Name OID SNMP OID (or branch, in dynamic) whose value replaces _nameOID_ in the name Value OID SNMP, network Final OID (or branch, in dynamic) that is read Macros OID SNMP, plugin List of OIDs (or branches) that take part in the operation, as _oid_N_ Value operation SNMP, plugin Formula with _oid_N_ that calculates the value shown in the preview; it is not used in the module created Server plugin SNMP, plugin Plugin that calculates the value on each run of the module; its fields accept the macros of the following table Satellite execution SNMP, plugin Equivalent command for when the wizard is launched from a satellite server WMI class WMI Class that is queried Query key field WMI Column of the response that identifies each row Query extra fields WMI Rest of the columns of the response that are needed Query filters (Scan / Execution) WMI Condition that limits the exploration and, separately, the execution of the module Field value WMI, network Column number whose value becomes the value of the module (0 = key field) Key string WMI, network Optional string that turns the value into 1/0 depending on a match; it is ignored when running from a satellite server Value operation WMI, plugin Formula with _f1_, _f2_… that calculates the value shown in the preview Satellite execution WMI, plugin Equivalent command for when the wizard is launched from a satellite server, with the wizard_wmi_module plugin

docs.title: Macro reference
docs.text:
Macro Replaced by Where it applies _nameOID_ Name obtained from Name OID Module name, SNMP components _oid_N_ In the preview, the value read; in the plugin fields and in the satellite execution, the OID at position N of Macros OID (with its index, in dynamic) Value operation, Server plugin fields, Satellite execution _o1_, _o2_… Value of the OID at that position of the plugin's OID list Operation field of the "Wizard SNMP module" plugin _FIELDNAME_ Value of the FIELDNAME column of the current WMI row WMI components _class_wmi_ WMI class of the component Server plugin fields and Satellite execution, plugin WMI components _field_wmi_N_ Value of the query extra field number N Plugin WMI components _f1_, _f2_… Value of the query extra field at that position Value operation and Operation field of the "Wizard WMI module" plugin _address_, _port_ Address and port the wizard was launched with Server plugin fields and Satellite execution (SNMP and WMI) _version_, _community_ SNMP version and community (v1/v2c) Server plugin fields and Satellite execution (SNMP) _sec_level_, _auth_user_, _auth_method_, _auth_pass_, _priv_method_, _priv_pass_ SNMPv3 credentials the wizard was launched with Server plugin fields and Satellite execution (SNMP) _namespace_wmi_, _user_wmi_, _pass_wmi_ WMI namespace and credentials the wizard was launched with Server plugin fields and Satellite execution (WMI)

Both wizards can also be launched on a monitoring policy instead of on a specific agent, with an important difference in how these macros are filled in: _address_ is left as it is, as a literal macro, so that each agent that receives the policy replaces it with its own address, just as in any other network module; the rest of the connection macros —version, community, SNMPv3 credentials, namespace and WMI credentials— are equally replaced by what was written when the wizard was launched, and stay fixed in the resulting policy module. With a policy that is applied to agents with different communities or credentials, it is advisable to review those values in each module after creating it.

Creating the plugin that runs a calculation of your own, instead of reusing the factory ones, is explained in 9.9 · Creating remote plugins.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Installing Pandora FMS is the easy part of the project. The hard part is deciding what it runs on, what is left out and who remembers all this in two years. This chapter covers the installation of the product, its requirements and the decisions worth making before running the first command, not after.

docs.title: What will be installed
docs.text:
The Pandora FMS online installer sets up the server, the Web console, the database and, optionally, a local EndPoint to monitor the server itself, all on a single machine. It is the monolith environment and it covers most cases.

The components do not have to live together, and each piece is installed separately afterwards to adapt the architecture: a database on a dedicated server, OpenSearch aside, one or several satellites for remote networks, or several nodes coordinated from the Command Center. This section explains the standard installation, and the variants are in Personalisation of the automatic installation.

The installable components of Pandora FMS are:

  • Server (pandora_server), with its database and the Tentacle server.
  • Web console (pandora_console).
  • EndPoint (pandora_agent and associated agents), on the machine to be monitored.
  • Satellite Server, a standalone server for remote networks.
  • OpenSearch, a log storage engine, optional.
  • Command Center (mf_server) and Cloud Server (cloud_server), for distributed environments.

The full requirements for each component are further down, in Minimum requirements. Read them before you start, because they are the difference between an installation that lasts for years and one that gives its first scare after three months.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before launching the online installation:

Requirement Detail Internet Access to the internet and to the official repositories of the distribution (RHEL / Rocky Linux / Ubuntu Server). curl Installed (it comes by default in almost every distribution). User root (or the equivalent with sudo). Operating system RHEL, Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux 9 or 10, or Ubuntu Server 22.04 or 24.04. More detail in Server requirements. Hardware Meet the minimum hardware requirements. RHEL 8 Licensed machine, subscribed to the standard repositories.

docs.title: Online installation of the server
docs.text:
If the machine has internet, this is the recommended path, and the online installer sets up the full server environment in a single step.

curl -SsL https://pfms.me/deploy_pandora_one | PANDORA_LTS=1 bash

The tool is requested through the Pandora FMS website and it works with RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux and Ubuntu Server. Red Hat is the recommended option, and the rest are supported with the versions given in the operating system table.

The command above performs a full installation, and the installer also accepts environment variables to customise it (database passwords, MySQL and PHP version, LTS or Feature Release channel, specific packages, and so on). They are all listed further down, in Personalisation of the automatic installation.

docs.title: Online installation of the EndPoint
docs.text: The EndPoint is the program that lives inside the monitored machine and it is not mandatory (remote monitoring exists), but it is the only way to obtain maximum detail: processes, inventory, local logs.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
The online installer works with Red Hat distributions (RHEL, Fedora, Rocky), SUSE/OpenSUSE and Debian/Ubuntu. It always installs from a TAR, never from an RPM, and it verifies that the downloaded package is an authentic EndPoint before configuring it against your server.

Minimum installation (GO EndPoint, LTS version):

export PANDORA_SERVER_IP='10.0.0.1'
curl -sSL https://pfms.me/agent-deploy | bash

The installer accepts environment variables to automate the installation or choose the package. They are all listed further down, in Personalisation of the automatic installation.

Supported architectures: x86_64 with binaries, while on x86, armv7l and aarch64 the script switches automatically to building from sources (PERL_SOURCES). On other architectures the process stops.

docs.title: MS Windows
docs.text:
The EndPoint is delivered as a .exe self-installer, so for the online installation, run PowerShell as administrator:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/pandorafms/LTS/PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe -OutFile ${env:tmp}\pandora-agent-windows.exe; & ${env:tmp}\pandora-agent-windows.exe /S --ip [SERVER_IP] --group [GROUP] --remote_config 1

And start the service:

NET START PandoraFMSAgent

The details of the manual and unattended installation are in Offline installation of the EndPoint.

docs.title: Installation of the satellite
docs.text: The Satellite Server is a headless server (no web interface) designed to discover and monitor remote networks that the Pandora FMS server cannot reach and where EndPoints cannot be installed either: network elements through SNMP/ICMP, Windows servers through WMI and Linux through SNMP. It runs up to 500 checks per second, it does not need a connection to the Pandora FMS database, and it sends the data as XML.

docs.title: Online installation
docs.text:
Supported operating systems: EL10 (RHEL 10 / Rocky Linux 10, recommended option), Ubuntu Server 22.04 and Raspberry Pi OS (Debian 12+, with the specific package for Raspberry).

export PANDORA_SERVER_IP='<IP or FQDN of the Pandora FMS Server>'
curl -Ls https://pfms.me/satellite-ent-deploy | bash

The installer accepts environment variables (release channel, default group, remote configuration, agent installation, and so on), listed further down in Personalisation of the automatic installation.

Compatibility

Satellite Server 785 is not compatible with earlier versions of Pandora FMS, so install it alongside a 785 or later environment, or you will have features that appear but do not operate.

docs.title: Installation of OpenSearch
docs.text:
Log collection is optional, and activating it requires an OpenSearch instance. It is not installed by default with the server: it is a separate deployment, and the recommendation is that it lives on a server independent from the Pandora FMS one.

curl -SsL https://pfms.me/pandorafms-opensearch-el | bash

The installer creates a node ready to use, with HTTPS and password authentication, and it is compatible with EL8, EL9 and Ubuntu 22.04 Server, and it accepts environment variables for the cluster name and the password, listed further down in Personalisation of the automatic installation.

Check that the node responds:

curl -X GET https://127.0.0.1:9200 -ku 'admin:<password>'

Change this password too, and apply the same rule as with the database: what is published protects nothing.

docs.title: Server requirements
docs.text:
Hardware. The values are minimums, calculated assuming that 80% of the modules store historical data and an average sampling of five minutes, with server, console and database on the same machine:

Hardware Small (≤ 1,000 modules) Medium (≤ 10,000) Large (≤ 30,000) Extra large (≤ 80,000) CPU 2 cores at 2 GHz 4 cores at 2.5 GHz 6 cores at 3 GHz 10 cores at 3 GHz RAM 4 GB 8 GB 16 GB 32 GB Storage 15K rpm or SSD ≥ 300 MB/s 15K rpm or SSD ≥ 300 MB/s SSD ≥ 300 MB/s SSD ≥ 300 MB/s Disk 40 / 60 GB 60 / 150 GB 120 / 250 GB 250 / 400 GB

If information is stored for more than one month, a historical database has to be deployed.

Virtualisation

In virtual environments, assign the machine an independent disk with reserved space and high speed. Putting the database on a shared, thin volume is the most reliable way to get a bottleneck that nobody will locate for weeks.

Above 80,000 metrics, a single node stops making sense, and it is time for distributed monitoring with multiple nodes (Command Center).

Software.

Software Requirements Operating system RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, RHEL 9 (recommended), Rocky Linux 9 (recommended), Ubuntu Server 22.04 and 24.04. Console PHP 8.4 from version 785, PHP 8.2 from 776 to 784, PHP 8 from 760 to 775, PHP 7.4 from 759 to 767 and PHP 7.2 from 729 to 758. Database Percona Server for MySQL 8 (recommended, especially above 4,000 agents), MySQL 8 or MySQL 8.4 from version 785. Browsers Chrome, Firefox, Opera and Edge. For interactive graphs and network maps, Firefox or Chrome. systemd Required since version 779. It comes installed and enabled on the supported OSs.

EL10 and Ubuntu

EL10 denotes the set of recommended systems: Rocky Linux 10, AlmaLinux 10 and Red Hat 10. Offline installation is not supported on Ubuntu Server, so do not choose it for a server without a connection, and for Command Center, avoiding Ubuntu is recommended.

Each LTS version of Pandora FMS supports specific operating system versions, so consult the OS version support policy before deciding.

Permissions.

Requirement Detail Installation user The server is installed as root. During the installation a pandora user is created and assigned to the root group, and it can be changed afterwards, bearing in mind that the Tentacle server will have to be reconfigured. There is also the installation with an unprivileged user, with a separate procedure. Console Apache needs read and execute permissions on the console files. config.php must have 600 permissions. Server Write permissions on /var/spool/pandora/.

docs.title: EndPoint requirements
docs.text:
The EndPoint can run on any machine with the minimum required operating system:

Component Operating system Pandora EndPoint 4.0 or later RHEL 10 / Rocky Linux 10, RHEL 6.x, 8 and 9, Fedora 34, CentOS 6.x, 7 and 8, AlmaLinux, SLES 11 SP1 or later, OpenSUSE 11.x or later, Debian 5.x or later, Ubuntu Server or Desktop 11 or later, Linux Mint, Elementary OS, Manjaro, HPUX B.11.11 or later with Perl 5.8, AIX 4.3.3 or later with Perl 5.8, AIX 7.1 and 7.2, BSD (NetBSD, OpenBSD, FreeBSD) with Perl 5.8, MacOS X 10.6 or later, Solaris 8 or later with Perl 5.8, Windows NT4, XP, 2000, 2003, 2008, 7, 8, 10, 11, 2012, Server 2016 and Server 2019. Pandora Android EndPoint 2.0 or later Android 6 or later. Pandora Embedded EndPoint 4.0 or later Embedded devices, requires compilation.

On *nix-type systems, systemd must be installed and started, and on UNIX environments, in addition:

Requirement Detail Perl 5.8 or later. Dependencies perl-YAML-Tiny-1.73-2, perl-Sys-Syslog and unzip. logrotate Configured for the EndPoint (next block). 
cat> /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent <<EO_LRA
/var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log {
        su root apache
        weekly
        missingok
        size 300000
        rotate 3
        maxage 90
        compress
        notifempty
        copytruncate
}
EO_LRA
chmod 0644 /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent

On Linux, the EndPoint runs as root to have all the features, and on Windows it runs with administrator permissions.

docs.title: Satellite requirements
docs.text:
Satellite Details Hardware (Windows) x64, minimum 2 cores at 2 GHz (4 recommended), minimum 6 GB of RAM (8 recommended), minimum disk 5 GB (10 recommended). Hardware (Linux) x64, minimum 2 cores at 2 GHz (4 recommended), minimum 4 GB of RAM (6 recommended), minimum disk 5 GB (10 recommended). Operating systems 64-bit Linux, 64-bit MS Windows. Dependencies fping, nmap, perl, pandorawmic (version NG 762 or later) and libnsl, plus snmp for SNMP.

On Rocky Linux 8 or later the EPEL repository has to be configured first, and on Windows, depending on the system version, Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable has to be installed.

docs.title: OpenSearch requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Detail Operating system Rocky Linux 8 / RHEL 8 / Ubuntu 22.04 (recommended). RAM Minimum 4 GB (dev/testing), 8 GB per instance recommended, although it has to be estimated according to the volume of data. CPU Minimum 4 cores. SWAP Disabled on the OpenSearch node or nodes. Storage 50 GB of system disk and 100 GB for OpenSearch. Connectivity From the Pandora FMS server and console to the OpenSearch API (9200/TCP) and between cluster nodes (9300/TCP).

A single node with these characteristics stores up to 1 GB of daily data for 30 days. For greater redundancy and capacity, a cluster is configured (minimum 3 nodes to guarantee data integrity) and the load is spread with a load balancer such as Keepalived.

docs.title: SIEM requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Detail OpenSearch OpenSearch database on a dedicated instance. Log collection Activated. Node resources Minimum 4 cores, 8 GB of RAM and 100 GB of SSD disk. SIEM instance A dedicated server is recommended for siemserver and siemevents. Licence With the SIEM feature enabled.

Once the requirements are met, SIEM is activated from the console in Management → Settings → System Settings → SIEM → Activate SIEM. On saving, the normalisation templates are created in OpenSearch and siemserver and siemevents are enabled on the corresponding servers.

docs.title: Security and network requirements
docs.text:
If the machine has security applications (EDR, XDR, antivirus), the Pandora FMS processes and paths have to be allowed, or you will see components dying with no explanation. Hand this list to the EDR administrator, exactly as it is.

For the server:

/var/spool/pandora
/usr/share/pandora_server
/etc/pandora
/var/log/pandora
/etc/tentacle
/usr/bin/pandora_server
/usr/bin/pandora_exec
/usr/bin/tentacle_server
/usr/bin/tentacle_client
/usr/bin/pandora_ha
/usr/bin/pandora_db
/usr/bin/pandora_manage
/usr/bin/pandora_revent
/usr/bin/pandora_encrypt_db
/usr/bin/pandorafsnmp
/usr/bin/pandorawmic
/usr/bin/clean_pandora_server
/usr/bin/clean_tentacle_serverd
/usr/bin/clean_tentacle_rmm

For the EndPoints:

/usr/share/pandora_agent
/usr/bin/pandora_agent
/usr/bin/pandora_agent_exec
/usr/bin/pandora_revent
/var/spool/pandora
/etc/pandora
/var/log/pandora
/usr/bin/tentacle_server
/usr/bin/tentacle_client
/usr/bin/clean_pandora_agent_daemon

For the Satellite Server:

/usr/bin/satellite_server
/etc/pandora
/var/spool/pandora
/usr/sbin/fping
/usr/sbin/wmic
/usr/bin/tentacle_server
/usr/bin/tentacle_client
/usr/bin/pandorafsnmp
/usr/bin/pandorawmic
/usr/bin/clean_satellite_serverd

In custom installations, the directory where it was installed has to be prepended to each path.

Ports. The complete table. When the network team asks what to open, this is the list:

Port Protocol Service Description Direction 80 TCP Console Web administration and API Browser → Console 80 TCP Console (API) API/CLI use Client → Console 80 TCP Command Center Command Center ↔ Nodes communication Command Center ↔ Node 162 UDP Server Trap reception Device → Server 443 TCP Console (API) API/CLI use Client → Console 443 TCP Command Center Command Center ↔ Nodes communication Command Center ↔ Node 3306 TCP Console and Server Database connection Server → DB 3306 TCP Command Center Node DB Command Center ↔ DB 4444 TCP Server Connection with Selenium GRID Server → Selenium 9995 UDP Server NetFlow probes nfcapd → Server 9200 TCP Console and Server OpenSearch (logs) Server → OpenSearch 9300 TCP OpenSearch Communication between cluster nodes Node ↔ Node 41121 TCP Agents Tentacle communication EndPoint → Server 41122 UDP Agents Remote actions over UDP EndPoint ↔ Server 41123 TCP Agents RMM feature EndPoint ↔ Server

For standard monitoring, the server also needs outbound access to what it monitors: 80/TCP and 443/TCP for web monitoring (WUX), 161/UDP for SNMP polling and ICMP for network checks.

docs.title: Values for the online installer
docs.text:
The basic run installs the full environment, and these environment variables customise it (values for RHEL and Rocky Linux):

Variable Function Default TZ Machine time zone Europe/Madrid DBHOST Database host 127.0.0.1 DBNAME Name of the database to create pandora DBUSER Database user pandora DBPASS User password Pandor4! DBPORT Database port 3306 DBROOTPASS Database root password Pandor4! SKIP_PRECHECK Skip the previous installation check 0 SKIP_DATABASE_INSTALL Do not install the database (use an external one) 0 SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS Skip kernel optimisation 0 MYVER MySQL version (80 or 84) 80 PHPVER PHP version (82 or 84) 84 PANDORA_SERVER_PACKAGE URL of the server RPM latest available PANDORA_CONSOLE_PACKAGE URL of the console RPM latest available PANDORA_AGENT_PACKAGE URL of the agent RPM latest available PANDORA_BETA Install beta (1) 0 PANDORA_LTS Install the LTS branch instead of Feature Release 1

On Ubuntu Server the list is similar but does not include the package variables for the server, the console and the agent, and it adds POOL_SIZE to set the MySQL memory (by default it is calculated automatically).

Example on EL10 with explicit values:

env TZ='Europe/Madrid' \
    DBHOST='127.0.0.1' \
    DBNAME='pandora' \
    DBUSER='pandora' \
    DBPASS='ChangeThisPassword' \
    DBPORT='3306' \
    DBROOTPASS='ChangeThisRootPassword' \
    MYVER=84 \
    PHPVER=84 \
    SKIP_PRECHECK=0 \
    SKIP_DATABASE_INSTALL=0 \
    SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS=0 \
    PANDORA_BETA=0 \
    PANDORA_LTS=1 \
    bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/deploy_pandora_one)"

Change the default passwords

Pandor4! is written in the public documentation. It is the first one anyone who knows the way in will try. Leaving it in place is not an oversight. It is leaving the door open and putting out the doormat.

docs.title: Kernel optimisation values
docs.text:
The online installer adjusts some kernel parameters. With SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS=1 it does not touch them, but it is worth knowing what is lost: they are settings designed to let the server withstand many simultaneous connections without the operating system becoming the bottleneck.

Parameter Default Set by Pandora What it does net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries 5 3 Retries when sending a TCP connection request before giving it up as failed. net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries 5 3 Retries when receiving the acknowledgement of a TCP connection. net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog 1024 65536 Maximum size of the queue of TCP connections pending acceptance. net.core.wmem_max 124928 8388608 Maximum send buffer for data per network connection. net.core.rmem_max 131071 8388608 Maximum receive buffer for data per network connection. net.core.somaxconn 128 1024 Pending connections in the socket listening queue. net.core.optmem_max 20480 81920 Maximum buffer for socket options.

Do not touch them by hand unless you know exactly what you are doing, and leave SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS=0 so the installer does its work.

docs.title: Installation on an external database
docs.text:
If there is a dedicated server for the database, the path is: create the database and the user, give it all permissions on that database and install with SKIP_DATABASE_INSTALL=1 and the connection values. Before installing, test the connection from the future Pandora FMS server, because discovering the firewall at two in the morning is avoidable with five minutes of checking.

env DBHOST='192.168.1.107' \
    DBNAME='pandora' \
    DBUSER='pandora' \
    DBPASS='ChangeThisPassword' \
    DBPORT='3306' \
    SKIP_DATABASE_INSTALL=1 \
    bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/deploy_pandora_one)"

Restrict the database user to the IP of the Pandora FMS server, so that if the password is compromised it does not work from anywhere else.

docs.title: External database installation for historical data
docs.text:
To deploy a dedicated database (historical data included) there is an online installer of its own. It only requires curl and a compatible system:

  • EL9: Rocky Linux 9.x or RHEL 9.x.
  • EL10: Rocky Linux 10 or RHEL 10.
  • Ubuntu: 22.04.
curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/db-deploy-el9 | bash

On Ubuntu:

curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/db-deploy-u2204 | bash

Supported variables:

Variable Description Default TZ Machine time zone Europe/Madrid MYVER MySQL version (8.0 or 8.4) 84 DBNAME Name of the database to create pandora DBUSER Database user pandora DBPASS User password Pandor4! DBROOTPASS Root user password Pandor4! SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS Skip kernel optimisations 0 POOL_SIZE Memory for MySQL (buffer pool) Automatic 
env TZ='Europe/Madrid' \
    MYVER=84 \
    DBNAME='pandora' \
    DBUSER='pandora' \
    DBPASS='ChangeThisPassword' \
    DBROOTPASS='ChangeThisRootPassword' \
    POOL_SIZE=4G \
    bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/db-deploy-el9)"

docs.title: Installation in a different path
docs.text:
To install the server in another path, the installer accepts --destdir:

./pandora_server_installer --install --destdir <destdir>

Then automatic start-up and the pandora_db maintenance script have to be configured in cron:

echo "\"<destdir>/usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_db\" \
 \"<destdir>/etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf\">/dev/null 2>&1"> /etc/cron.hourly/pandora_db

docs.title: Installation with an unprivileged user
docs.text:
The installer can run with an unprivileged user:

./pandora_server_installer --install --no-root --destdir /opt/pandora

That user must have write permissions on the path given in --destdir.

docs.title: Values for the online installer
docs.text:
Variable Function Default PANDORA_SERVER_IP IP or FQDN of the Pandora FMS server — PANDORA_AGENT_PACKAGE Package type: GO, PERL or PERL_SOURCES, or a direct URL GO PANDORA_AGENT_PACKAGE_TYPE Dependencies to install when the package is a URL GO PANDORA_AGENT_RELEASE Version: LTS (STABLE) or BETA STABLE PANDORA_SKIP_CONFIRMATION Unattended installation with no confirmations (1=yes) 0 
export PANDORA_SERVER_IP='10.0.0.1' \
       PANDORA_AGENT_PACKAGE=GO \
       PANDORA_AGENT_RELEASE=STABLE \
       PANDORA_SKIP_CONFIRMATION=1
curl -sSL https://pfms.me/agent-deploy | bash

docs.title: Installation in a different path
docs.text:
The EndPoint can be installed entirely in a defined directory: logs, configuration, binaries and man pages are left there.

./pandora_agent_installer --install /opt/pandora

docs.title: Installation with an unprivileged user
docs.text:
It can also run with a user other than root, for example with the pandora user:

./pandora_agent_installer --install /home/pandora pandora

When specifying a custom user, the installation must go to a location where that user has write permissions. The pandora user is disabled by default, so to use it, it has to be given a valid shell in /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Values for the online installer
docs.text:
Variable Default Description PANDORA_SERVER_IP — Mandatory. IP or FQDN of the server the satellite points to. VERSION LATEST Installation channel: LATEST or LEGACY. TZ Europe/Madrid Time zone in IANA format. REMOTE_CONFIG 1 Configuration management from the console (1=yes). INSTALL_AGENT 1 Installs the EndPoint on the satellite itself (1=yes). PANDORA_GROUP Servers Default group of the satellite agents. SKIP_KERNEL_OPTIMIZATIONS 0 Omits the kernel performance settings (1=omit). RHEL_CHECK_SUBSCRIPTION 1 Verifies active subscriptions on RHEL (1=yes). PANDORA_SKIP_CONFIRMATION 0 Unattended installation with no confirmations (1=yes). PANDORA_BETA 0 Installs the development beta version (1=yes). SATELLITE_SERVER_PACKAGE Auto-selection Custom URL of the Satellite Server tarball. 
env TZ='Europe/Madrid' \
    PANDORA_SERVER_IP='192.168.10.10' \
    VERSION='LATEST' \
    bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://pfms.me/satellite-ent-deploy)"

In addition, the manual installation requires setting the server_ip token in /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf pointing to the Pandora FMS Server, and starting satellite_serverd. In Windows installations, the path must be given without quotes, because with quotes the installer does not interpret it correctly.

docs.title: Values for the online installer
docs.text:
Variable Default CLUSTER_NAME pandora_opensearch OPENSEARCH_PASS P4nd0r4!FMS 
env CLUSTER_NAME='pandora_opensearch' \
    OPENSEARCH_PASS='ChangeThisPassword' \
    bash -c "$(curl -SsL https://pfms.me/pandorafms-opensearch-el)"

For advanced configurations (nodes, templates, user management and cluster) there is specific OpenSearch documentation, and the installer only sets up a basic working node.

docs.title: Offline installation
docs.text: For environments without an internet connection, and it is not supported on Ubuntu.

docs.title: Offline installation of the server
docs.text:
The compatible systems are RHEL 9 / Rocky Linux 9 and RHEL 10 / Rocky Linux 10.

Steps:

  1. Have a clean instance with the hardware requirements and the supported operating system.
  2. Download the offline package for the operating system from the support portal (available for LTS and previous LTS versions).
  3. Upload the tarball to the server.
  4. Unpack it and run the installer:
tar xvzf <offline_package>.tar.gz
cd pandora_packages/
./pandora_deploy_enterprise_local_el9.sh

On EL10 the script is pandora_deploy_enterprise_local_el10.sh, and when the process finishes, the Web console is accessed with the admin user and the pandora password.

docs.title: Manual installation on Linux
docs.text:
Once the dependencies are installed and the package downloaded, it is unpacked and the installer is run:

tar -xvzf pandorafms_satellite_server_X.XNG.XXX_x86_64.tar.gz
cd satellite_server/
./satellite_server_installer --install

Then /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf has to be edited and the server_ip token set with the address of the Pandora FMS Server, and the service is started with:

systemctl start satellite_serverd

The log is in /var/log/satellite_server.log.

docs.title: Installation on MS Windows
docs.text: The installer (signed since version 762) includes Nmap and the Visual C++ Redistributable from MS Visual Studio 2015-2022. It is run with administrator rights, the licence is entered, the server address and the scanning rules are configured, and the machine is restarted. If WMI queries fail, the Satellite Server service has to be run with an Administrator account.

docs.title: Offline installation of the EndPoint
docs.text:
The EndPoint is installed from the tarball package, valid for any Unix/Linux/macOS, and it does not require compilation.

tar xvzf pandorafms_one_agent_linux-latest.tar.gz
cd unix
./pandora_agent_installer --install
systemctl start pandora_agent_daemon

libnsl may have to be installed manually, and if the sources are used (.src.tar.gz), there are additional Perl dependencies, among them YAML::Tiny and Thread::Semaphore. On FreeBSD and NetBSD the file location and the start-up script change: the EndPoint stays in /usr/local/bin/pandora_agent, its script in /usr/local/etc/rc.d/pandora_agent, the configuration in /usr/local/etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf, and pandora_agent_enable="YES" has to be added to /etc/rc.conf.

After the installation, /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf has to be edited to point to the server and, as a recommendation, to activate remote configuration:

sed -i "s/^remote_config.*$/remote_config 1/g" /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf
systemctl enable pandora_agent_daemon

docs.title: Unattended Windows
docs.text:
The Windows installer supports unattended mode since EndPoint version 5.1:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S

Custom path:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S /D=C:\PFMS_agent

Parameters written to the EndPoint configuration: --ip (server_ip), --group (group), --alias (agent_alias) and --remote_config (remote_config). Example:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S --ip 192.168.0.59 --group Applications --alias Mifunne --remote_config 1

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Once the installation is finished, open the console at http://<server>/pandora_console/ and confirm that it loads the login screen, where the initial user is admin with the pandora password.

Warning

Change the password on the first login, and if you installed with a custom user or a different path, check that the services start before you call it done. The fault that is not reviewed today turns into an incident on Monday.

docs.title: Uninstallation
docs.text: The installers are not copied during the installation, so their --uninstall cannot be used afterwards. Uninstallation has to be done by hand: these are the files and folders each component leaves behind and the commands to remove them (as root). If several components live together on the same machine, do not delete the shared directories until they have all been removed.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• Binaries in /usr/bin: pandora_server, pandora_exec, pandora_supervisor, pandora_db, pandora_ha, pandora_manage, pandora_revent, pandora_encrypt_db, braa, pandorafsnmp, pandorawmic, pandora_iot_server, pandora_netflow_server, tentacle_server, tentacle_client, clean_pandora_server, clean_tentacle_serverd and clean_tentacle_rmm.
  • Libraries and utilities: /usr/share/pandora_server.
  • Services: /etc/systemd/system/pandora_server.service, pandora_ha.service, tentacle_serverd.service, tentacle_rmm.service, pandora_iot_server.service and pandora_netflow_server.service.
  • Tasks and rotation: /etc/cron.hourly/pandora_db and /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_server.
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf, pandora_server.env, pandora_server_extra.env, /etc/pandora/conf.d and /etc/tentacle.
  • Data, logs and PID: /var/spool/pandora, /var/log/pandora and /var/run/pandora_supervisor.pid.
systemctl stop pandora_server pandora_ha tentacle_serverd tentacle_rmm \
  pandora_iot_server pandora_netflow_server
systemctl disable pandora_server pandora_ha tentacle_serverd tentacle_rmm \
  pandora_iot_server pandora_netflow_server
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/{pandora_server,pandora_ha,tentacle_serverd,tentacle_rmm,pandora_iot_server,pandora_netflow_server}.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /usr/bin/{pandora_server,pandora_exec,pandora_supervisor,pandora_db,pandora_ha,pandora_manage,pandora_revent,pandora_encrypt_db,braa,pandorafsnmp,pandorawmic,pandora_iot_server,pandora_netflow_server,tentacle_server,tentacle_client,clean_pandora_server,clean_tentacle_serverd,clean_tentacle_rmm}
rm -Rf /usr/share/pandora_server
rm -f /etc/cron.hourly/pandora_db /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_server

And, if no other component remains, the shared configuration and data:

rm -Rf /etc/pandora /etc/tentacle /var/spool/pandora /var/log/pandora

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
It depends on how it was installed:

  • RPM (RHEL / Rocky Linux): it is removed with the package manager.
dnf remove pandorafms_console
  • Tarball (Ubuntu): it was copied to /var/www/html/pandora_console and it left its log rotation behind.
rm -Rf /var/www/html/pandora_console
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_console

The console shares the /var/spool/pandora/data_in directory with the server (collections, conf, md5, netflow). Do not delete it if there is a server, and it does not touch the database, which goes separately.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
The installation creates the pandora database and the pandora user, and if MySQL or Percona only served Pandora FMS:

systemctl stop mysqld
mysql -u root -p -e "DROP DATABASE pandora; DROP USER 'pandora'@'localhost';"
dnf remove 'Percona-Server*'        # RHEL/Rocky. On Ubuntu, apt remove percona-server-server or mysql-server
rm -Rf /var/lib/mysql /etc/my.cnf /etc/my.cnf.d

If the database is on another server or holds data from other applications, limit the operation to DROP DATABASE and DROP USER.

docs.title: Satellite
docs.text:
• Binaries in /usr/bin: satellite_server, tentacle_client, pandorafsnmp, wmic, pandorawmic and clean_satellite_serverd.
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf, satellite_server.env, satellite_server_extra.env, /etc/pandora/satellite_plugins and the agents directory /etc/pandora/conf.
  • Start-up: /etc/init.d/satellite_serverd (with its link in /etc/rc.d) and /etc/systemd/system/satellite_serverd.service.
  • Rotation, logs and temporary files: /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_satellite, /var/log/satellite_server.log and /var/spool/pandora/tmp/satellite_server.
systemctl stop satellite_serverd
systemctl disable satellite_serverd
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/satellite_serverd.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /etc/init.d/satellite_serverd
rm -f /etc/rc.d/rc?.d/S90satellite_server
rm -f /usr/bin/{satellite_server,tentacle_client,pandorafsnmp,wmic,pandorawmic,clean_satellite_serverd}
rm -Rf /etc/pandora/satellite_plugins /etc/pandora/conf /var/spool/pandora/tmp/satellite_server
rm -f /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf /etc/pandora/satellite_server.env /etc/pandora/satellite_server_extra.env
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_satellite /var/log/satellite_server.log

The /opt/pandorafms/perl5 directory of the satellite is shared with other components, so delete it only if none remains installed.

docs.title: EndPoint
docs.text:
On Linux and Unix it leaves:

  • Binaries in /usr/bin: pandora_agent, pandora_agent_exec, pandora_revent, tentacle_client and clean_pandora_agent_daemon.
  • EndPoint home: /usr/share/pandora_agent (plugins, collections, commands, ref).
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf and pandora_agent.env.
  • Start-up: /etc/systemd/system/pandora_agent_daemon.service (or the script in /etc/init.d).
  • Rotation, logs and man pages: /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent, /var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log, /usr/share/man/man1/pandora_agent.1.gz and tentacle_client.1.gz.
systemctl stop pandora_agent_daemon
systemctl disable pandora_agent_daemon
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/pandora_agent_daemon.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /usr/bin/{pandora_agent,pandora_agent_exec,pandora_revent,tentacle_client,clean_pandora_agent_daemon}
rm -Rf /usr/share/pandora_agent
rm -f /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.env
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent /var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log
rm -f /usr/share/man/man1/pandora_agent.1.gz /usr/share/man/man1/tentacle_client.1.gz

If there is a server or satellite on the same machine, do not delete /etc/pandora or /var/spool/pandora entirely.

MS Windows does include an uninstaller, which in unattended mode runs like this:

"%ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\uninst.exe" /S

Or from the EndPoint binary:

pandoraagent.exe --uninstall

docs.title: Introduction and architecture
docs.text: Pandora FMS is not something you understand by looking at a screenshot of the console. You understand it when you know where every piece of data comes from, who brings it in and where it is stored. This chapter walks that path: what can be monitored, with which piece, and which topology is needed for the data to arrive. The following parts cover each topic in depth. This is the map.

docs.title: Introducing Pandora
docs.text:
Pandora FMS monitors systems, networks, applications and services. The unit it works with is not the machine, it is the agent: a logical container of modules. It is attached to a group and, optionally, to one or more IP addresses. An agent can receive local data (from an EndPoint installed on the machine) or remote data (from a network check), and the usual thing is that it receives both.

Every module stores a single metric, with a unique name inside its agent. Its value is interpreted through thresholds: that is where the NORMAL, WARNING and CRITICAL states come from, plus the UNKNOWN state when a module stops receiving data. Those states generate events and trigger alerts. Everything else in this chapter is a way of feeding that mechanism.

docs.title: Remote monitoring
docs.text:
The server does it: it goes out and asks. Nothing is installed on the device, you only need network visibility towards it. It is the natural route for network devices and for anything that will not take software on top.

With SNMP you query the OIDs the vendor exposes. And you listen to the traps the device sends on its own, without anyone asking for them. On MS Windows machines remote checks are done through WMI, with credentials. And for everything else there are the classic network checks: ICMP (ping, latency, jitter), TCP with challenge and response to confirm a port is answering, and static web checks, which verify availability and content, not a full user transaction.

One difference worth being clear about from the start: a remote check lives or dies by the network. If there is no path to the device, there is no data, and no amount of retries from the console will fix it. The topologies further down exist for those cases.

docs.title: Monitoring with EndPoints
docs.text:
The EndPoint is the program installed on the machine that runs the checks from the inside. That is where the real power is. Any data you can obtain with a command or a script is within reach, inventory included: installed software, disks, services. And it can act on the system when asked to: start a service, delete a temporary file.

The EndPoint packs everything from the interval into a single XML file and sends it to the server with Tentacle, on port 41121/TCP. The default interval is 300 seconds. Since version 784 some checks accept much shorter intervals, down to 15 seconds: ICMP (latency and ping) and numeric SNMP ones. Asynchronous modules never go below five minutes, and the console warns you if you try to force it.

With EndPoints there are three working modes for the modules that arrive in the XML. In learning they are created on their own. In normal they are only created if they are declared in the console. In self-disabled it works like learning, but the agent shuts down if everything turns unknown. Choosing one or the other is an operations decision, not a configuration detail: it defines who is in charge of what gets monitored, the machine or the console.

docs.title: Monitoring cloud environments and APIs
docs.text: Cloud providers and external services will not let you put an EndPoint inside, and often they will not let you probe them over ICMP either. The way in is the API they publish, and for that Pandora FMS uses its module and plugin library: there are plugins for specific cloud platforms and a generic API request plugin (ApiRequest) for whatever does not have one. The result is stored as one more module, so it inherits thresholds, alerts and everything above. If the service has an API, it can be monitored. If it does not, what gets checked is the availability of the access point.

docs.title: Application monitoring (Discovery)
docs.text:
Discovery is the leap from monitoring what you already know to finding out what is out there. The wizard explores the network, finds machines and devices, identifies the operating system and applies a monitoring template to whatever it finds, which starts reporting without going through the creation form. Beyond the network, Discovery is used to inventory virtual environments, databases and applications before monitoring them.

The value is in the start: on a large network, creating hundreds of devices by hand is weeks of work with guaranteed oversights. Discovery turns that into a short review and a list of exceptions.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Monitoring without presenting the data is collecting for its own sake. Reports, dashboards and visual consoles are the part that turns information into decisions: trends, SLA compliance and capacity planning.

Every user can build their own dashboard with widgets: graphs, status summaries, maps. Reports group data from several agents and modules, with different calculations and formats. For what has not happened yet there are prediction modules: capacity, trending and arithmetic operations on other modules. The capacity one answers the useful question: how many days until the disk fills up, if everything stays the same. They are there to warn before the incident, not to explain it afterwards.

docs.title: The event console
docs.text:
The event console shows, in real time, what is happening. It is a snapshot, not a history. Events are classified by severity (from maintenance and informative up to critical, through warning) and they are the raw material of alerts, which add notification and escalation.

It may look like an old feature in a modern tool, and it is. It is also still the fastest way to answer the question "what has broken?" without opening twenty graphs. Many tools in the market do not have an event console like this one, and you notice it exactly when you are in a hurry.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Pandora FMS collects logs from multiple sources in a single console, sorted by the timestamp at which they were processed, keeping the original timestamp from the file as well. The text is stored as it is, with no structure, in OpenSearch, which is what supports the volume.

The syslog server analyses the system log of the machine where it is installed and the log server lets you correlate logs and fire alerts on them. It is the raw material for SIEM and the troubleshooting tool for when the problem is not in the state of a module, but in what the system was saying while it was failing.

docs.title: Network topics (Netflow, SNMP, IPAM, NCM, remote shell)
docs.text:
This groups what looks at the network as the subject, not as the medium:

  • NetFlow and sFlow analyse traffic in real time from the data the devices send (or from a probe with port-mirroring). The collector listens on 9995/UDP. It is the way to know who is talking to whom and how much, when SNMP only tells you how many packets cross an interface.
  • SNMP is the query protocol and the one that receives traps (162/UDP) for all network equipment.
  • IPAM (version 731 or later) manages the IP addresses of your networks: it discovers the hosts of a subnet, detects when they stop answering, resolves their names and makes a guess at the operating system. It works whether or not those machines are monitored.
  • NCM (Network Config Management) goes into devices over Telnet or SSH to back up their configuration, restore it and run commands, with templates per vendor and model. It needs the Heavy server running.
  • The remote shell covers manual access: a web terminal for equipment managed over Telnet or SSH, and graphical remote control with Pandora RC for Windows, Linux and macOS.

docs.title: SIEM
docs.text:
A SIEM collects, filters, normalises, correlates and presents security events. What Pandora FMS adds to the concept is that collection is already done. The logs that feed the SIEM are the same ones the platform already gathers. The security event engine builds on that previous work, in place of setting up a second system alongside it.

For the installation it is recommended that EndPoints are at least on version 783 to make the most of all the features. The SIEM is activated from the console and enables its own servers. With it come the normalisation templates, the security events and their correlation.

docs.title: RMM
docs.text:
RMM stands for Remote Monitoring and Management. In Pandora FMS it is the piece that allows scheduling tasks from the console and having the agents run them locally, reporting the result afterwards. It comes into play from version 778 and relies on three components: the RMM agent, the RMM server (which stores the scripts and the executions) and the Tentacle RMM service, which connects the two over port 41123/TCP.

It is the basis for the remote management of many machines at once: distributing software, applying changes and keeping a record of what was executed on each machine, without going into them one by one.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Pandora FMS started as a monolith (server, console and database on the same machine) and that is still the most sensible way to begin. But no component is condemned to live next to the others: they are separated when the network, the volume or the organisation ask for it. The architecture decision is not made by the product, it is made by your infrastructure.

docs.title: Console
docs.text: The web console is the visible face and also the door to automation: the same console you use by hand is the one that exposes the API for scripts to work with. Permissions live there (groups, profiles and tags) and decide who sees and who administers what. And it can be deployed on several servers, to spread the load or to serve different groups of users.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The Pandora FMS server is a single application with several specialised servers inside, running as concurrent processes and with their own number of threads. Their configuration lives in pandora_server.conf, in /etc/pandora.

These come enabled by default:

  • Data Server: processes the XML packages sent by EndPoints and turns them into data, events and alerts.
  • Network Server: runs remote checks: ICMP, TCP, SNMP, WMI, web checks and prediction modules.
  • Heavy Server: takes care of the tasks that need more muscle: plugins, NCM and inventory.
  • Network High Performance Server: moves ICMP and SNMP in bulk, designed for high volumes.
  • Discovery Server: explores the network and runs scheduled discovery tasks.

These come disabled, to be switched on only when needed:

  • SNMP Console: receives SNMP traps through snmptrapd and processes them.
  • Event Server: relates events and fires the associated alerts.
  • Alert Server: runs all monitoring alerts, so that a slow alert does not hold up the checks.
  • Log Server: the one that allows generating alerts from logs.
  • Syslog Server: analyses the syslog of the machine where it is installed and stores it in OpenSearch.
  • NetFlow Server: collects and processes NetFlow and sFlow flows.
  • WUX Server: runs complex web transactions in a real browser, with Selenium Grid.
  • SIEM Server and SIEM Event Server: normalise logs and generate security events.
  • MADE Server: the anomaly detection engine (Monitoring Anomaly Detection Engine).
  • RMM Server: hosts the scripts and the executions that RMM agents download.
  • Mainframe Server: monitoring of mainframe environments (z/OS).
  • Sync Server: goes out to fetch data from isolated networks, as explained in the topologies below.

There is a third group, the servers that depend on the master server:

  • Policy Manager: applies policies to agents. When a change affects hundreds of agents at once, the work goes into a queue of operations and this server is the one that serves it.
  • Migration Server: moves agents between the nodes of a Command Center, taking the tasks from a prioritised queue. It only exists in Command Center environments.
  • Autoprovision Server: the auto-provisioning server. It receives agents that arrive with no destination and decides which node they are created in, according to the configured strategy: round-robin, the least loaded node, or custom rules (by alias, by subnet…).

All three start alongside the master of a node or of a Command Center, which is where their work makes sense.

The list has been getting shorter with the versions. Since 784 several servers were grouped into others to stop wasting memory on processes that were no longer needed. Prediction, WMI and web checks went into the Network Server. Plugins, NCM, inventory and export went into the Heavy Server. And ICMP and SNMP went into the Network High Performance Server.

On load distribution: there can be several servers of the same type working at the same time. Within each type one is the primary and the rest are secondary, but they all work. If a secondary goes down, the primary absorbs what it had assigned. High availability acts on another layer: with two nodes in active/passive, the one still alive takes on all the work. The status and load of every server are visible from the console itself, because the system monitors itself like it monitors anything else.

docs.title: EndPoint
docs.text:
The EndPoint is the program running on the monitored machine. We have already seen it in the first half of the chapter: it collects data locally, packs it into an XML and sends it to the server over Tentacle at every interval. When it has no direct path to the server, it can send its data through a satellite server or through another EndPoint acting as a proxy.

It is the piece you have to install, update and, now and then, uninstall without leaving a trace. The installation part is in Installation. What matters here is that its presence is the border between local and remote monitoring.

docs.title: Satellite server
docs.text:
The satellite server is an autonomous server installed close to the remote network. It does not need to connect to the database: it runs the checks and sends the results as XML over Tentacle, just like an EndPoint would. It is the answer when you cannot reach some devices over the network and cannot install anything on them either.

It has two virtues worth knowing. The first is speed: it can run up to 500 checks per second, and although it only sends data to the server every so often, if it detects a state change it reports it immediately. The second is that it discovers itself: it finds devices over SNMP or WMI, creates the corresponding agents and generates interface, traffic, CPU, memory and disk modules with no intervention.

And it is managed remotely. The satellite asks the server every few seconds (every 30 by default) whether there are changes in its configuration or in that of the agents it has discovered. It applies what arrives from the console. It is the satellite that starts the connection, so no port has to be exposed in the remote network. And when it needs to be reached from the server, for instance for the SNMP wizard, it is also the satellite that opens a reverse SSH tunnel.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Everything the platform collects ends up in the database, the component everything else depends on. Pandora FMS works with MySQL, MariaDB or Percona, and in practice two of them are used: the real-time one and the historical one, to which data is moved once it no longer needs to be queried by the second.

The database can be replicated for high availability in active/passive or set up in an active/active cluster with load balancing. Together with the historical database, this is where you decide how much detail you keep and for how long: cheap on disks, expensive in slow queries.

docs.title: Command Center
docs.text:
The Command Center is the layer above all of the previous. It manages several Pandora FMS installations (the nodes or instances) from a single interface: seeing them together, synchronising their configuration and operating on all of them. Every node keeps its own database and its own server. The Command Center does not replace them: it coordinates them. That is how you reach hundreds of thousands of devices without looking at them node by node. And how you can provide multi-company service from a single access point.

Synchronisation goes in two directions. The Command Center queries the database or the API of each node for what it administers: agents, modules, alerts, policies. And it receives by replication what is continuously generated, such as events.

Users, groups, templates and tags live on both sides, because they have to be where they are used. That said, it is an advanced environment with its own requirements: it is installed on RHEL 8 or Rocky Linux 8.

docs.title: Topologies, diagrams and monitoring models
docs.text: We have reached the point that decides everything else. The topology is not chosen out of taste. It follows from a single question: in which direction can the connection be established. The rest of the chapter is the answer, case by case.

docs.title: Accessible networks
docs.text:
This is the comfortable case and the one covering most installations. There are two variants, and they can live together:

  • The Pandora FMS server reaches what it monitors, so it can do centralised remote monitoring.
  • Or the EndPoints installed on the machines reach the server, so they report without a problem.

If your network meets one of the two (or both), you need nothing else from this section.

docs.title: Networks that are hard to reach
docs.text:
Here the connection exists, but not in the direction that would suit you. It is solved with an intermediate piece. Which one depends on where the break is:

  • If the server cannot reach the network, a broker agent is deployed on a machine with access to both sides.
  • If the EndPoints cannot reach the server, the proxy mode of the EndPoints is used, or a satellite server acting as an intermediary.
