With several exporters sending flows to the same server, "Netflow source IP" in 192.168.10.1 limits the view to the flows that router exported, even if the filter touches neither the source nor the destination of the traffic. Leave the advanced filter expression empty for the exporter field to be applied.

docs.title: Top view
docs.text:
Operation → Monitoring → Network → Netflow top view. Four breakdowns over the same period: Applications, Network protocols, Netflow sources (which router and which interface have exported the most flows, with the last time each IP was seen) and Connections (the Top-N of connections that in previous versions was in the live view). The percentages of a Top-N do not have to add up to 100. The period can be chosen, but this screen does not allow applying an IP, port or advanced expression filter.

Which application consumes the most bandwidth this week

"Applications" breakdown and period the last week: the table sorts the detected applications by traffic volume, from highest to lowest, without restricting the result to a network such as 192.168.10.0/24.

docs.title: Network usage map
docs.text:
Operation → Monitoring → Network → Network usage map. It represents traffic as a map of connections between nodes, instead of a table or a chart: each line between two points represents observed traffic according to the period and the advanced filter applied. Here senders or receivers can be chosen, as well as the number of results, and the map's own filters can be saved. It does not show countries or geolocate the nodes, even if a GeoIP database is configured.

Seeing the outgoing connections of a network at a glance

With "Data to show" in Top talkers, 10 results and advanced filter src net 192.168.10.0/24, the map shows the connections between the nodes of that traffic; it does not place the destinations on a geographic map.

docs.title: Monitoring and alerting on a filter
docs.text:
Monitoring a filter turns its traffic into agent modules. It is enabled from the filter editor itself, with "Enable Netflow monitoring". With the Netflow server enabled (netflowserver 1) and automatic agent creation enabled, the agent Netflow_<filter name> is created and three modules are added; if the agent already exists, it is reused:

Module What it measures Throughput (<filter>_throughput) Total traffic of the filter (module with the bps label) Throughput status (<filter>_throughput_status) Normal, warning or critical, according to the configured thresholds Top 10 (<filter>_throughput_data) The 10 IPs with the most traffic inside the filter, with their throughput and a ratio with respect to the configured maximum, in text

The interval of this monitoring is set per filter —five minutes to start with—. The status module distinguishes normal (0), warning (1) and critical (2) when comparing the traffic of the IPs with the configured thresholds. The form labels the maximum traffic in bytes per second and presents the thresholds as percentages, but the status calculation does not apply a consistent conversion between the units of the throughput and those of that maximum. A threshold value that guarantees the expected result cannot be deduced from those labels; it is advisable to check the status with known traffic before associating an alert. These modules accept alerts like any other module; their configuration is explained in Alerts and notifications.

Checking the monitoring before associating an alert

In a filter on network 192.168.10.0/24, set the interval to 300 seconds and check that the agent Netflow_<filter name> receives the throughput module, the status and the Top 10. Compare the status value with measured traffic before using it as an alert condition; the form alone does not ensure the equivalence between bytes/s and bits/s.

docs.title: Reports and dashboards
docs.text:
Four chart types —area graph, summary, data table and Top-N of connections— are available as report elements, each one with its own filter, period, resolution and maximum number of values; see 5.2 · Reports for the rest of the report elements and how to combine them. The Netflow widget of dashboards goes further: it offers the nine Netflow chart types —the four previous ones plus circular mesh, host detailed traffic, sources, applications and protocols— and also a network usage map, with its own period, aggregation, "Data to show" (Top listeners/Top talkers) and maximum number of values; see 5.1 · Dashboards.

Weekly report of the Top-N of connections

Top-N of connections report element, filter on network 192.168.10.0/24, weekly period, maximum 10 values: every week the report records which connections concentrated the most traffic.

docs.title: Netflow data on another machine: remote nfdump
docs.text:
When the traffic volume is high and it is convenient to store the capture files on a dedicated disk, on another machine, the query service can run nfdump over SSH against that remote machine instead of doing it locally. It is enabled on the Remote tab of the Netflow configuration, with the connection host, port and user. The query service runs as a system service under the root user, so the SSH key that has to be authorised beforehand in the authorized_keys of the remote user is the one of root on the machine where that service runs, with no password: the service has no way of entering it interactively. The connectivity check that feeds the status indicator also uses batch mode (without asking anything on screen) and a short timeout, of a few seconds, before taking it as down. With remote query enabled, the status indicator of the Basic tab adds a second line that says whether that SSH connection is reachable at that moment.

In this setup, the collectors and nfexpire keep running wherever it corresponds: if the capture files live on the remote machine, the purge by age also has to be scheduled there, for example with a cron task that calls nfexpire with the same maximum lifetime configured in the console.

Storing the capture on a dedicated storage server

With the public key of root of the Pandora FMS server already added to the authorized_keys of a user in 192.168.10.50, "Enable Remote Nfdump" is enabled with host 192.168.10.50, port 22 and that same user: the operation views keep working the same, but every query is resolved by nfdump on that remote machine, not on the Pandora FMS server itself.

docs.title: Netflow in the Command Center
docs.text: In an architecture with a Command Center, each node still has its own Netflow query service, with its own collectors and its own configuration. The Command Center does not centralise the flow data —neither do the nodes, which query them on demand—: when Netflow data are requested from the Command Center console, it calls the remote API of each node involved and joins the responses, without the traffic itself going through the Command Center.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions are not identical on all screens. The Explorer and the Network usage map check agent read (AR); the Live view and the Top view accept read (AR) or write (AW). Managing the list of Netflow filters requires AW, while the creation and editing form checks write on resources (RW) and, for an existing filter, its group. Saving or modifying the map's own filters requires AW. A map filter is not equivalent to a Netflow filter assigned to a group.

Requirement Detail Explorer and Network usage map Agent read (AR) Live view and Top view Agent read (AR) or agent write (AW) Manage the list of Netflow filters Agent write (AW), with the list limited to the accessible groups Create or edit a Netflow filter Write on resources (RW); to edit an existing one, also access to its group Save or modify the map filters Agent write (AW)

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
A module_plugin often needs something more than the command written in its configuration: a script, a binary, a configuration file of its own. Copying that file by hand on every agent that is going to use it works the first time and becomes a problem the second, when it has to be updated on twenty machines at once. A collection is Pandora FMS's answer to that problem: a package of files that is uploaded once to the Web console and deployed, compressed, to the EndPoints that need it.

A collection can be assigned to an individual EndPoint, to a monitoring policy —which propagates it to all its agents— or to a Satellite server. The Web console prepares the package; each recipient is in charge of receiving it. This chapter goes through how a collection is created and edited, how it is applied and synchronised, and what changes depending on where it is assigned from.

docs.title: Creating and managing a collection in the console
docs.text:
In the Web console, collections are created in Management → Configuration → Collections. The creation form asks for a name, a group, a description and an optional short name: if it is left empty, the console generates one with a timestamp (fc_<timestamp>). That short name is not a cosmetic detail, it is the identifier that later appears as a directory in the console and on each EndPoint, so it is worth setting it by hand and making it say something.

Requirement Detail At least one file in the collection An empty collection does not get to generate the compressed package Shape of the short name Only letters, numbers, _ and -; if left empty, one is generated automatically with a timestamp ZIP compression utility on the console server Needed to generate the package when applying changes Compressed package size not above the configured limit See the warning below

With the collection already created, editing adds its resources: uploading a file, creating a directory or creating a text file that is edited directly from the console itself, without going through the administrator's computer. All of that is stored on the console side, in an attachment directory with the short name of the collection.

There is a size limit for the final compressed package (collection_max_size). When applying the changes, the Web console first creates a temporary ZIP. If it exceeds the limit, it does not publish it in the remote configuration path and does not compute its MD5; the collection is left pending application. Its content has to be reduced and the changes applied again.

A collection for an Apache plugin

The apache_plugin collection holds a single file, the script pandora_apache_v1r1.pl that Pandora FMS brings installed by default: it is the package that an Apache module_plugin expects to find on the EndPoint before it can run.

docs.title: Synchronising the changes: applying a collection
docs.text:
Adding or modifying resources of a collection does not deploy it on its own: the Web console shows a yellow triangle icon in the list next to any collection with changes pending application. When it is applied, the console server compresses the whole directory into a ZIP, computes its MD5 and leaves both files in the remote configuration path, ready for the EndPoints to download on their next cycle.

A collection can be in three states: pending application (the changes have not been published), correct (the ZIP and the MD5 are up to date) and lost directory, if the directory of the collection disappears from the console side.

The short name of the collection does not only identify the package: it is also the name of the base directory of the collection on the console side (/pandora_console/attachment/collection/<short_name>), which can hold subdirectories without any problem.

docs.title: Assigning a collection to an EndPoint
docs.text:
In the Web console it is assigned from Resources → Manage agents, the Collection tab of the EndPoint. The tab lists the collections available according to the group of the EndPoint and a button to add them; the synchronisation state of each one is shown with a warning icon if it is still empty or has not been applied.

Without remote configuration enabled on the EndPoint, the Web console cannot deliver the collection to it —this was already explained in Monitoring with EndPoints— so that requirement is not repeated here. A few minutes after it is assigned, the EndPoint itself should appear listed in the agents tab of the collection, confirming that it already has it.

Assigning the Apache collection to an EndPoint

With apache_plugin already created and applied, it is assigned to the Servidor-Apache-01 EndPoint from its Collection tab: on the next remote configuration cycle, the EndPoint downloads the package.

docs.title: Where the collection ends up on the EndPoint
docs.text:
Each EndPoint keeps its collections in a subdirectory of its own inside its collections folder, with the short name of the collection as the subdirectory name: on Windows, %ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\collections\<short_name>; on Unix or on the Go EndPoint, /usr/share/pandora_agent/collections/<short_name> in a package installation, or in general the collections/<short_name> subdirectory next to the configuration file of the agent itself. That each collection has its own subdirectory is no coincidence: it prevents two different collections from stepping on each other if they share the name of some file. A module_plugin references a file of the collection with its full path.

Uncompressing the package does not work the same on all EndPoints. The Perl EndPoint (Unix) and the Windows EndPoint invoke an external unzip utility —on Windows it is included from version 3.2 of the EndPoint, inside %ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\utils—. The Go EndPoint, on the other hand, uncompresses in memory with its own standard library, without depending on any external binary installed on the system.

As for the transfer mode the package arrives with, there is no restriction of its own for collections: they use the same mode configured for the rest of the remote configuration of the EndPoint (see Monitoring with EndPoints), with no distinction for collections in particular.

Full path of a file of the collection

The script of the apache_plugin collection on a Unix EndPoint installed from packages is left in /usr/share/pandora_agent/collections/apache_plugin/pandora_apache_v1r1.pl, and that is how the module_plugin that uses it references it.

docs.title: How it stays synchronised: MD5 control
docs.text:
The MD5 of the collection package is computed in the Web console when applying changes and is sent to the EndPoint along with the ZIP. On every cycle, the EndPoint compares that remote MD5 with the one it has stored locally: if they match, it does nothing; if they do not match, it downloads and uncompresses the whole collection again.

This has a practical consequence worth keeping in mind: if the files of a collection already deployed on an EndPoint are edited by hand, those changes survive as long as the collection does not change in the console. As soon as it changes, the next synchronisation overwrites the whole collection and those local modifications are lost.

The cleanup of collections that no longer appear in the configuration does not guarantee an immediate deletion. The Perl EndPoint runs check_collections on every cycle, except in debug mode; it skips the deletion if there are broker agents or it cannot open the collections directory. The Go EndPoint also checks on every cycle, but it skips the entries whose name starts with . and may fail to read or delete files. On Windows, the collections check calls purgeDiskCollections, which skips the deletion if there are broker agents. When the assignment is removed from the Web console, it stops appearing in the corresponding remote configuration. Deleting a collection from the Web console does not guarantee either that it disappears immediately from the EndPoint: the removal of the local files depends on the cleanup running and being able to complete.

docs.title: Collections and monitoring policies
docs.text: From the Web console, a collection can also be assigned to a whole monitoring policy instead of to an individual EndPoint, with the same underlying mechanism but propagated to all the agents of the policy. It is managed from the Collections tab of the policy: adding or removing an existing collection and applying the policy so that the change queue propagates it to all its agents. The rest of the management of a policy —applying it, the change queue, its other tabs— is outside this chapter; see Monitoring policies.

docs.title: Collections on the Satellite server
docs.text:
A Satellite server can also receive collections from the Web console: Management → Servers → Manage satellite server, Collections icon: a list of collections available with an actions column to add or remove them. When a collection is added, the Web console writes file_collection <short_name> in the remote configuration of the Satellite and updates the MD5 of that configuration file. The Satellite compares that MD5 to detect changes in its configuration; when processing file_collection, it queries the MD5 of the package of the collection separately. If it differs from the local one, it downloads the ZIP and uncompresses it with the configured utility. They are not the same MD5, nor the same code that an EndPoint uses to receive collections.

With the configuration included in the package of the Satellite server (agent_conf_dir /etc/pandora/conf), the collections are left in /etc/pandora/satellite_collections/. The path is derived from agent_conf_dir/../satellite_collections and can be changed with collection_dir. The public collections wiki also states that path.

docs.title: Collections from the Command Center
docs.text: Since Pandora FMS 729 OUM, collections can also be managed centrally from the Command Center Web console: Centralised management → Agent management, the Collections tab. The operation is the same as in the console of a node; the only thing that changes when operating from the Command Center is that synchronisation towards the nodes is done through its own synchronisation mechanism between node and Command Center.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The management of collections in the Web console —creating, editing, applying, assigning— requires agent write permission (AW) on the group of the collection. The list of available collections is filtered by the groups where the user has that permission, plus the All group.

Requirement Detail Viewing the list of collections It is filtered by the groups with agent write permission (AW), plus the All group Creating, editing, applying or assigning a collection Agent write permission (AW) on the group of the collection

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text: There is a question that appears in any systems department sooner or later, almost always at a bad moment: "and what do we have?" Not what is green or what alert went off this morning, but what machines there are, with which processor, what software they have installed, who has an account on them and what services they start on boot. Answering that by hand is archaeology: open a session here, look at a uname over there and pray nobody installed something they should not have. The inventory in Pandora FMS exists so that archaeology is not necessary: it collects that data on its own, from every monitored machine, and leaves it available to query and export.

docs.title: What inventory is
docs.text:
Inventory is the part of Pandora FMS that answers "what is there", not "how is it doing". It is a distinction worth making clear from the start: a monitoring module has thresholds, statuses and alerts; an inventory record does not. Nobody is going to get a notice because a machine has version 1.2 of a library installed. Inventory is a photograph, and its value lies in being able to compare photographs: what changed since yesterday, what new software appeared, which user was created without anyone knowing.

That is why inventory is independent of monitoring. It is collected separately, stored separately and queried separately, even though it lives in the same console and feeds the same reports. A machine can be perfectly monitored and hold not a single inventory record, and the other way round.

Data can be collected in two ways:

  • Locally, with the EndPoint installed on the machine. The EndPoint runs the inventory plugins and sends the result.
  • Remotely, with the inventory modules that the Pandora FMS server runs against a machine on the network: WMI queries, SSH commands or any script that returns the expected format.

Inventory feeds listings and reports: from a list of software installed across the whole fleet to a report of configuration changes on a network device. That is covered further down.

docs.title: Inventory modules: the catalogue
docs.text:
Everything starts with an inventory module. It is the piece that defines what is collected, and it has three data that matter: a name, the operating system it applies to and a list of fields separated by semicolons. When the module collects data, each line of the result is split by those fields and shown as a table. If the format says Model;Size, the console knows that the first column is the model and the second one the size.

Pandora FMS ships a fairly broad default catalogue of modules, split by operating system. These are the main ones:

Operating system What can be inventoried Linux Processor, memory, video and network cards, disks, CD-ROM, installed software, start-up services, file systems, processes, users, IP addresses and routes Windows All of the above plus monitors, motherboard, installed patches, printers, installed services, Microsoft products and keys (MS-Products, product_ID, product_key) Solaris Processor, memory, network cards and software Cisco Device configuration, interfaces (through a local script or over SSH) and general information Android Installed software

The catalogue is what the console offers; what the EndPoint collects on its own and what is requested remotely is covered in the next two sections.

There is one detail that costs more than one lost hour and that is worth saying out loud: the operating system of the module has to match the one of the EndPoint. If a module is marked as Windows and you try to assign it to a Linux EndPoint, it will not appear in the list. It is not a console error: the module is meant for another system.

Where all this is managed: Management → Configuration → Inventory modules.

docs.title: Local inventory with EndPoints
docs.text: The local path is the most convenient one when the EndPoint is already installed: the machine looks at itself and sends the result. There are no ports to open and no one's credentials to store.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
On Linux, the EndPoint carries a plugin called inventory. It is enabled with one line in the pandora_agent.conf configuration file:

module_plugin inventory 1 cpu ram video nic hd cdrom software init_services filesystem users route

The line reads in three parts. First, enabling the module. Then a number that is how often, in days, it runs: if set to 0, inventory is sent on every EndPoint run. And at the end, the list of objects to collect. If only the number is left, everything available is collected:

module_plugin inventory 1

The objects the plugin understands are: cpu, ram, video, nic, hd, cdrom, software, init_services, filesystem, process, users, ip, route and kernel.

Requirement Detail lshw or hwinfo installed The plugin uses them for hardware. With neither of the two, only software, start-up services, file systems, processes and routes are collected root permissions Some objects (for instance, the user list or the hardware) need elevated privileges

The plugin records on the machine itself when it last ran, so the interval in days is respected even if the EndPoint starts many times a day.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
On Windows, local inventory is not enabled with a single line, as on Linux. Here each inventory object is a module of its own, and each module calls its own script. The EndPoint brings the sample in the configuration file (commented out); you uncomment what you want to use and restart the EndPoint. Each module has this shape:

module_begin
module_plugin cscript.exe //B //t:20 "%PROGRAMFILES%\Pandora_Agent\util\cpuinfo.vbs"
module_end

The scripts the Windows EndPoint brings cover, each one, one object:

Object EndPoint script Processor cpuinfo.vbs Memory raminfo.vbs Disks diskdrives.vbs CD-ROM cdromdrives.vbs Video card videocardinfo.vbs Network cards ifaces.vbs Monitors monitors.vbs Printers printers.vbs Installed software software_installed.vbs Microsoft products and KBs ms_products.exe Users userslogged.vbs Product key and ID productkey.vbs, productID.vbs

One detail to look at before leaving it like that: the factory sample adds module_absoluteinterval 7d to every module, which makes inventory run once every seven days, regardless of the EndPoint interval. If inventory has to follow the normal EndPoint frequency, that line is removed. A weekly inventory goes stale fast.

docs.title: Local modules appear on their own
docs.text: Here is the practical difference with remote inventory, and it is worth underlining because it saves a fair amount of work: local modules are not assigned by hand in the console. It is enough that the module exists in the catalogue with the right operating system and that the run is defined in the EndPoint file. When the first data arrives, the console creates the module in the agent's record and leaves it visible on its Inventory tab.

docs.title: Creating your own local modules
docs.text:
Besides the ones that come as standard, you can create your own inventory modules for Linux and Windows. The procedure is the same as for remote, with two exceptions: the Interpreter and Code fields are left empty, and a script is needed that returns an XML with this structure:

<inventory>
  <inventory_module>
    <name>MODULE_NAME</name>
    <type>generic_data_string</type>
    <datalist>
      <data>DATA1;DATA2;DATA3</data>
    </datalist>
  </inventory_module>
</inventory>

The name has to be exactly the same one given to the module in the console, and each <data> is a line with the fields separated by ; as declared in the Format.

The script is declared in pandora_agent.conf as one more plugin: the EndPoint runs the command and puts its output as is into the XML it sends to the server, so the script only has to print the <inventory> block on standard output. On Linux, a shell script and the line that launches it look like this:

#!/bin/sh
# /etc/pandora/plugins/mi_inventario.sh

echo "<inventory>"
echo "  <inventory_module>"
echo "    <name>MyInventory</name>"
echo "    <type>generic_data_string</type>"
echo "    <datalist>"
echo "      <data>one;two</data>"
echo "      <data>three;four</data>"
echo "    </datalist>"
echo "  </inventory_module>"
echo "</inventory>"

# pandora_agent.conf
module_plugin /etc/pandora/plugins/mi_inventario.sh

The EndPoint plugins directory (/etc/pandora/plugins) is in the PATH, so the script can also be called by its name (module_plugin mi_inventario.sh). On Windows, the line follows the same pattern as the standard modules, with module_begin and module_end, and the script prints the same XML:

# pandora_agent.conf
module_begin
module_plugin cscript.exe //B //t:20 "%PROGRAMFILES%\Pandora_Agent\util\mi_inventario.vbs"
module_end

And the warning about order: the module has to be created in the console before restarting the EndPoint, or the data will arrive and there will be nowhere to store it.

docs.title: Remote inventory: creating the module and assigning it
docs.text: The remote path is the one used when there is no EndPoint on the machine: a network device, a server on which nothing is to be installed or a machine only reachable over SSH. Here the one doing the work is the Pandora FMS server, which runs the module script against the target and stores the result.

docs.title: Creating the module
docs.text:
It is done in Management → Configuration → Inventory modules, with the Create button. The fields of the form are these:

Field Detail Name Mandatory; the identifier of the module Description Free text OS Mandatory; it has to match the one of the target Interpreter The interpreter the script runs with (Shell, Perl…). It is left empty only for local modules Format Mandatory; the fields the module returns, separated by ; Block Mode Switch; the module result is treated as a single block (see further down) Script mode Choose between Script mode (a Script path is given) and Use inline code (the Code is written directly)

The classic warning, and it still holds: if the Format is left empty, the module is not saved and what was written is lost. It is the field that gets forgotten the most and the one that annoys the most when it is forgotten.

docs.title: What the script has to return
docs.text:
Here is the difference with local inventory, and it is worth having it clear because it is the one that breaks the first attempts: the remote script does not return an XML. The XML with <inventory> is the EndPoint's business; the remote module returns plain text, with one record per line and the fields separated by ;, in the same order as the module Format. The server stores that output as is and the console paints it as a table, using the Format as header.

The script receives as arguments the target (the value of the Target field) and then either the custom fields in the order they were created or the user and password. With that it queries the remote machine and writes one line per element.

A minimal example: a module with Format Field1;Field2, Interpreter /bin/sh and this Code:

#!/bin/sh
# $1 is the target; then come the custom fields or the user and password
target="$1"

# ... the query against $target goes here ...

echo "one;two"
echo "three;four"

That leaves two records, one per line, with two fields each. A real module does exactly the same, only it fills each line with whatever the query returns: the Windows CPU module that ships with Pandora prints one line per processor with name;speed;description, and the Cisco one writes a single line with IP;hardware;serial number;IOS.

If the module is in Block Mode, the output is not split into records: it is stored whole as a single text block, which is what is later compared in the diff view.

docs.title: Assigning it to the EndPoint
docs.text:
The assignment is done in the agent's record, on the Inventory tab (Management → Resources → Manage agents → agent → Inventory). The creation form asks for:

Field Detail Module The inventory module to add; only those matching the EndPoint OS appear Interval How often it runs (one hour by default) Target IP or name of the machine the inventory is taken from Use custom fields Replaces user and password with fields of its own, with a name Username and Password Target credentials; they accept EndPoint custom field macros

With Use custom fields, fields are created with a name, given a value and marked It's a password on those that have to be stored obfuscated. Those fields are passed to the script in the same order they were created. Once the module is assigned, the table on the tab allows you to Force an immediate run (useful to avoid waiting for the interval), edit it or delete it.

Underneath, the server builds the command with the interpreter, the script path or the inline code, the target and the credentials (or the custom fields), and runs it with a configurable timeout. If the command fails, the inventory of that cycle is simply not updated.

docs.title: Viewing inventory data
docs.text: There are two ways to look at inventory, and each one serves a different purpose.

docs.title: The agent's Inventory tab
docs.text:
In an agent's view, the Inventory tab shows all its modules, one below another. At the top there is a Module selector, a Date selector (Now by default) and a search box. Each module is painted as a table, with the Format as header and a Total of records at the foot. It is the view for looking at one particular machine calmly.

The date selector needs an explanation, because it puzzles you the first time. A date only appears when there were changes. Pandora FMS stores inventory only when the data changes from the last time, so if a machine has been the same for a week, the selector will not have one entry per day. It is a design decision, not a failure: storing the same photo every hour would be noise.

docs.title: The global view
docs.text:
In Operation → Monitoring → Inventory the inventory of the whole fleet is seen at once. The filters are group (with the option to include subgroups), agent, module, free search, order by agent, date and agent status.

By default the view is in Basic info mode, which shows one row per agent with its general data: alias, IP, group, operating system, version, interval, last contact, custom fields… When a specific module is chosen, the table changes and shows the data of that module, with a timestamp column and an agent column to know whose each row is.

The Export to CSV button downloads whatever is filtered at that moment, with the CSV separator configured in the console.

docs.title: Changes generate events
docs.text: Every time the inventory of a module changes, the server generates a configuration event with the additions and the removals: which record appeared and which one disappeared. It is the raw material of change reports, and also the reason why a very busy module (the process list, for example) can flood the console with events. That is what the blacklist explained in the inventory maintenance section is for.

docs.title: Differences between inventory versions
docs.text:
There are modules whose result makes no sense split into rows. The configuration of a network device, for example: it is a text block and what matters is comparing it with the one from the previous run, not reading it line by line as a table.

That is what Block Mode is for. When it is enabled on a module, its result is stored whole as a text block, and in the agent view a Diff view button appears next to the module name:

That view puts the two versions in two columns and highlights what changed. It is the tool to answer "has anyone touched this router since last week?".

docs.title: Inventory alerts
docs.text:
Inventory also serves to watch what should not be there. That is what inventory alerts are for, configured in Management → Alerts → Inventory alerts.

The idea is the same as the one of the rest of Alerts and notifications, with one fundamental difference: they do not fire on a monitoring module, but on the content of the inventory of a group of agents. They are therefore global: they apply to a group, not agent by agent.

The form has these fields:

Field Detail Name and Description Identification of the alert Group acl Visibility of the alert Inventory modules The module whose content is watched Condition How it is decided whether it fires: Match, Black list or White list Time threshold Minimum time between triggers Action What runs when it fires Alert groups The groups of agents it is evaluated on (the real condition) Disable event If enabled, the alert does not also generate an event

Group acl and Alert groups have to be told apart carefully, because both talk about groups and they do not mean the same: the first is who can see the alert, the second is which agents it applies to. A slip here leaves the alert with no effect or firing where it should not.

The three conditions work like this:

  • Match. The module fields are filled in (for example, the name and version of a software) and it fires when one line of the inventory matches all of them. The fields accept regular expressions, and an empty field is equivalent to "any value" (.*). It is the condition for "tell me if this particular version of this program shows up".
  • Black list. A module field is chosen and a list of values is written, one per line. If the inventory contains any of them, it fires. It is the condition for "this should not be installed".
  • White list. The same, but the other way round: the inventory value has to be in the list, and if it is not, it fires. It is the condition for "only these are allowed".

And Disable event has its charm when inventory triggers many alerts at once: it prevents each one from also generating an event and leaving the events console like a Christmas tree. The alert still fires and runs its action; what is saved is the event.

These alerts are the way to detect vulnerable versions of a program, unauthorised software or user accounts nobody should have.

docs.title: Inventory in reports and policies
docs.text:
Inventory does not live isolated: it feeds reports and it can be deployed through policies.

Under reports there are four elements that pull from inventory:

  • Agent inventory, the list of agents with their general data.
  • Module inventory, the list of modules with their data.
  • Inventory, the full inventory with filters.
  • Inventory changes, the additions and removals recorded.

The mechanics of templates and reports are covered in Reports.

And under policies, inventory modules can be applied to groups of agents just as a monitoring module is applied, with its interval. On the Inventory tab of the agent, the modules that come from a policy are marked with an icon. Policies are explained in Monitoring policies.

docs.title: Inventory maintenance
docs.text:
Two settings worth knowing so that inventory does not become a problem of space or of noise.

The first is deletion by age. The Max. days before delete inventory data field is in Management → Settings → System Settings → Performance, 21 days by default. Past that term, the server starts deleting the oldest inventory history. If it has to be kept longer for audits, it is raised; if the database has to be slimmed down, it is lowered.

The second is the changes blacklist. There are modules whose content changes on every run (the process list is the textbook example) and that would therefore generate a configuration event every time. To avoid it, those modules are marked in a list and their changes stop generating events.

The list is in Management → Settings → System Settings → General setup, on the Behavior tab, inside the Events section. It is a double selector: on the left are the modules that are out of the blacklist and on the right the ones that are in the blacklist, and they are moved from one side to the other with the arrows.

From the factory, the processor, the processes and the security module already come excluded, in their Linux and Windows versions.

With this, inventory is complete: it is collected on its own, it is queried at a glance, it warns when something does not add up and it does not fill the database more than necessary. Which is exactly what is asked of a tool that answers the question "what do we have?".

docs.title: Planned downtime
docs.text: A system patch, a backup that starts at two in the morning or a scheduled reboot of the hypervisor are windows in which the infrastructure behaves oddly on purpose. Monitoring, which does not know that, fires alerts by the dozen. A planned downtime is how you tell the web console, in advance, which stretch of time it should not take seriously.

docs.title: What a planned downtime is
docs.text:
The web console lets you create planned downtimes from Management → Alerts → Scheduled downtime. The idea is simple: a window of time is defined, along with what happens inside it, and the Pandora FMS server applies that state while the window is open.

Depending on the Type chosen, the downtime does one of four things: disable the selected EndPoints, disable their modules, disable only the alerts of those modules or mark them as quiet. In all four cases, when the downtime starts and when it ends, the server generates an informational system event, one of those that appear in blue in the events console. That trace is the practical difference from disabling an EndPoint by hand: the downtime is temporary, scheduled and reversible, and the event records that it ran and when.

Do not confuse the two gestures. Disabling an EndPoint by hand and forgetting to enable it again is a classic of the trade, and it stays in the reports as a gap with no explanation. A planned downtime, on the other hand, switches itself off when the time comes, and the periods it covers are marked as valid in the availability and SLA reports, as explained further down.

docs.title: Creating a planned downtime
docs.text:
The creation form asks for little and brings the most convenient values already filled in:

Field Default value Detail Name empty Mandatory and unique; two downtimes cannot have the same name Group All Group the downtime will belong to Description empty Free text to document the window Type Quiet The four options are detailed in their own section Execution Once With an initial slot from the current time to the current time plus one hour

Before saving, the console checks that the dates are coherent: the start before the end, the start time before the end time and the correct day range in the periodicities that use one. A repeated name or an inverted slot does not pass the filter.

One option changes the meaning of "creating in the past". It is Allow create scheduled downtimes in the past, and it lives in the general settings, in the behavior section. It is enabled by default. With it enabled, a downtime whose window has already passed can be registered: the downtime does not run, because the server does not see it start, but its existence is reflected in the availability reports and in the SLA calculations. It is useful to document a maintenance that was done without having created the downtime on time. Anyone who reads that downtime in the list should not expect to see it move to "Running".

docs.title: Execution modes: once, periodically and cron
docs.text:
The Execution field accepts three modes, and each one hides a different form.

Once. The most direct one: start date and time and end date and time. The downtime starts when the start arrives, applies during the slot and ends on the end date. It is the option that solves a one-off maintenance.

Periodically. It repeats the window over time. The Type Periodicity can be Weekly or Monthly. In the weekly one the days of the week are chosen; in the monthly one, a range of days of the month (for example, from day 20 to day 10 of the next month). In both cases a time slot is set with From hour and To hour, and the slot is allowed to cross midnight. Here the Expiration Date also appears, with a Never switch: if it is disabled, the downtime stops running past that date. It is the only mode that offers expiration; Once and Cron from/to do not show it.

Cron from/to. The most flexible mode and the least friendly one. Two conditions are defined, one for the start (Cron from) and one for the stop (Cron to), and each one is made of five fields: Hour, Minute, Month day, Month and Week day. Each field is set as Any or Custom. Watch the order: in the form the fields go Hour, Minute, Month day, Month, Week day, but the expression the console stores —and that you will see in the Configuration column of the list— starts with the minute (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). The server checks every minute whether the expression matches the current minute: it requires an exact match, not an approximate one.

Two examples to fix the format:

  • 0 2 * * 1 starts on Monday at 02:00.
  • */15 9-17 * * 1-5 starts every fifteen minutes between 09:00 and 17:00, from Monday to Friday.

The expression is stored as is and the server evaluates it on every cycle. It is worth reviewing the condition after creating it, because it is the piece that decides when the downtime starts and when it stops.

docs.title: The four types of downtime
docs.text:
The Type drop-down offers exactly four options. It is worth reading them calmly, because two of them are similar in name and do different things.

Type What it does When it ends Disabled Agents Disables the selected EndPoints and, with them, all their modules Re-enables only those that were not already disabled by hand Disable Modules Disables the selected modules, including those already disabled before the downtime Re-enables the modules the downtime covered Disabled only Alerts Disables the alerts of the selected modules, without disabling the module Reactivates the alerts Quiet Marks the EndPoint or the modules as quiet: they keep collecting data, but generate no events and fire no alerts If it quieted the EndPoint, it goes back to its previous state; if it quieted modules, they are reactivated even if they were already quiet

The first row deserves a nuance. Disabled Agents acts on the EndPoints and drags all their modules with it. The other three act on the modules, not on the whole EndPoint. And Disabled only Alerts disables no module: what it switches off are the alerts of those modules.

The detail that generates the most questions is the preservation of the manual state. If an EndPoint was already disabled (or quiet) by hand before the downtime started, when the automatic end comes it respects it: it stays as it was. With modules there is a nuance worth having clear: the automatic end of the server re-enables everything the downtime covered, including what was already switched off by hand. The difference is in who ends it: if you stop it by hand from the console, only what the downtime itself switched off is reverted, in agents as well as in modules.

docs.title: Adding agents and modules
docs.text:
The creation form already includes the element selector: the EndPoints and the modules affected are chosen in the same creation step, with no need to create an empty downtime and add them afterwards. The selector is a dual panel: on the left the Available agents, on the right the Selected agents, with the Add and Remove buttons to move them from one side to the other. If there are no agents selected yet, the modules are not filled in and the console warns with a Select agents first.

The panel filters do most of the work:

  • Group limits the list of available agents to the chosen group.
  • Recursion decides whether the agents of the subgroups are also included: recursion is respected. The "All" group resolves to the user's groups and only adds subgroups when recursion is enabled.
  • Module data type filters the modules by their data type, with All types by default.
  • Common modules shows only the modules that are present in all the selected agents. It is the quick way to apply the downtime to a shared module without going agent by agent.

A practical rule that saves trouble: in Quiet, if no specific module is selected, the whole EndPoint is quieted; in Disabled Agents and Disabled only Alerts, leaving the module list empty applies the downtime to the agent as a whole. In Disable Modules, on the other hand, at least one module has to be chosen: with no modules selected the downtime starts but does nothing. And in that type the selector does not filter by status: disabled modules appear too.

Elements are saved as they are added and can be removed one by one from the same screen.

docs.title: Managing the list: filter, stop, copy, delete and export
docs.text:
The downtime list shows one row per downtime with these columns: Name (Ag.) (the name and, in brackets, how many agents are affected), Description, Group, Type, Execution, Configuration, Running, Affected, Stop downtime, Copy, Edit and Delete. At the top are the filters Search, Group, Between dates, Execution type, Agent, Module and the Do not display previous or stopped downtimes checkbox, plus the Export to CSV button.

The Between dates filter only makes sense with Once downtimes; the periodic ones and the cron ones are not searched by slot. And the order of the list is not the creation date: it is sorted by execution type and by start date, so the creation date is a fact of the record, not the criterion of the table.

The Configuration column sums up the window in the format that applies:

Mode How it is shown Once 2026-10-01 13:57 to 2026-10-01 14:57 Periodically, weekly Weekly: Thu (00:00:00-23:59:59) Periodically, monthly Monthly: From day 20 to day 10 (08:00:00-09:00:00) Cron from/to Start condition: * * * * * - Stop condition: * * * * *

You can act on every row. While a downtime is Running it cannot be edited and the Delete button shows as N/A; what is available is Stop downtime, which cuts the execution on the spot and answers with a "Downtime has been stopped successfully". Copy duplicates the downtime to reuse its configuration, and Export to CSV dumps the list with the filters applied.

One notice is left, the one that appears when the console detects downtimes created with old, malformed formats: "WARNING: There are malformed scheduled downtimes" and the question "Do you want to migrate automatically the malformed items?". On accepting, the console splits each malformed downtime into two halves, labelled [1/2] and [2/2], so that the window that crossed from one period to another is expressed in a valid way.

docs.title: How it runs inside
docs.text:
The execution is not done by the console: it is done by the Pandora FMS server. In an installation with several servers, only the master applies the downtimes, so that they do not step on each other.

Every 60 seconds, the server goes through the downtimes and checks whether it is time to start or stop any of them. The check depends on the execution type: a Once downtime compares the current time with its slot; a Periodically one looks at the day and the time; a Cron from/to one evaluates its two expressions against the current minute. When a downtime starts, the server applies the state and writes the system event "Server \<server> started planned downtime: \<name>"; when it ends, it writes the corresponding "stopped".

Requirement Detail Pandora FMS server running Without a server there are no downtimes; the console only defines them Master server In installations with several servers, only the master applies the downtimes One cycle every 60 seconds The server checks every minute whether it is time to start or stop one Server clock Cron conditions are compared by the minute with the server time Downtime not entirely past A downtime whose window has already passed does not start; the permission to create it in the past is read by the console, not by the server

docs.title: What changes in reports and SLA
docs.text:
Here is the reason for everything above. The periods covered by a planned downtime are considered valid: they do not penalise the SLA and do not muddy the availability, because the system knows the infrastructure was down on purpose. Without that mark, a one-hour maintenance would read as a one-hour outage.

The reports sum up a period with several states according to the Priority mode, which decides whether the OK state or the unknown one prevails when they coincide. That setting is not from this screen and it is explained in detail in Reports; here it is enough to know that a well-created downtime protects the calculation.

If the past option is enabled, the downtime is recalculated backwards in time, so that a window already closed keeps counting in the reports that cover it. In service reports, a downtime that affects any element of the service is considered to affect the whole service, and malformed downtimes stay out of the calculation. The detail of services is in Business and service monitoring.

docs.title: The Scheduled Downtime dashboard widget
docs.text:
Planned downtimes also have their place in dashboards. The widget is called Scheduled Downtime in the catalogue and shows the name of each downtime, its configuration, whether it is running and the elements affected. It accepts a filter by group, pagination and export to CSV and JSON.

How a widget is added to a dashboard, which sizes it accepts and how it is placed is explained in Dashboards; here it is only noted that it exists and what it shows.

docs.title: Outside the console: API and CLI
docs.text:
The console is the convenient path, but not the only one. The API allows creating, editing and deleting downtimes, besides adding agents, adding modules and removing agents from a downtime that already exists, with operations such as planned_downtimes_edit, planned_downtimes_deleted, planned_downtimes_add_agents and planned_downtimes_delete_agents. The general operation of the REST API and the webhooks is covered in Integration and automation.

From the server command line, the command appendix offers --create_downtime to create it, --add_item_downtime to add elements, --get_all_planned_downtimes and --get_planned_downtimes_items to list, --stop_downtime to stop it and --set_planned_downtimes_deleted to delete it. There is a nuance worth keeping in mind: stopping a periodic downtime in execution does work from the web console, but the CLI rejects it. The command answers with an "[ERROR] … cannot be stopped" and an "[INFO] Periodical and running planned downtime cannot be stopped". If a periodic one that is running has to be cut, it has to be done from the interface, not from the CLI. The command catalogue is in Quick command cheat sheet.

A broad-brush alternative is left for whoever does not want to create one downtime per case: the CLI allows enabling or disabling whole groups of EndPoints with --enable_group and --disable_group. It serves for a quick, global deactivation, but it does not schedule the return and does not leave the downtime mark in the reports. That is what the planned downtime is for.
