docs.title: Automatic agent distribution and installation
docs.text:
Installing an EndPoint on one machine is a bit of work. Installing it on fifty is an afternoon. Installing it on two hundred, across different operating systems and with passwords nobody wrote down, is one of those tasks that get postponed until there is no choice left. The Deployment Center in Pandora FMS exists for that: you give it a list of targets, a credential and an EndPoint version, and it makes the target connect, download the installer, run it and leave the agent reporting. No machine-by-machine sessions and no copying the same installer twenty times.

The idea makes more sense if you say it the other way round. The Deployment Center does not push anything: it does not launch an installer against the machine from the server. What it does is tell the target to download the installer from a Tentacle server and run it itself. That is a small difference in the explanation and a huge one in practice, because it shapes the whole network: the target must be able to reach the Tentacle, not the other way round. Everything else (the scan, the credential, the target state) revolves around that connection.

The lab behind this chapter deployed EndPoints on three real machines: Rocky Linux 9, Ubuntu 22.04 and Windows 11. All three ended up reporting to the console. The details, and a few nuances, are on the pages that follow.

docs.title: Introduction: what it solves and when to use it
docs.text:
The Deployment Center is the screen from which EndPoints are distributed to machines that have already been located, or can be located on the network. It brings together in one place the four pieces that used to be handled by hand: the installer (the EndPoints repository), the credential used to access the machine, the target list and the task that runs the deployment. What used to be copying the installer and logging into each machine becomes one row per machine and a button.

In the console it is under Management → Discovery → Host & Devices → EndPoint deployment, and the page is titled Deployment center. Use it when several machines meet three conditions: they can be reached over SSH or WinRM, they can reach a Pandora FMS Tentacle server, and they share an EndPoint version you want installed. That is the typical case for a group of Linux servers, a set of Windows workstations or a branch network with a nearby Discovery server. It also works to reinstall an EndPoint that was left half-done, with the precautions described in Deploying the EndPoint.

It is not for everything. If the machine has neither SSH nor WinRM, the center cannot get in and you will have to install it by hand or with the online installer in 1.1 (Installation). If the network prevents the target from reaching the Tentacle, the deployment will fail even with the right credential: the problem will not be authentication, it will be the return path. And if there is only one machine, or two, going through the console may take longer than running the installer once.

Nor should it be confused with the pieces around it. The center installs the EndPoint; it does not configure monitoring. Modules, policies and alerts come later, through 2.1 (Monitoring with EndPoints) and 2.10 (Monitoring policies). And it does not replace network discovery in 2.4 (Network discovery with Host & Devices): discovery finds machines; the Deployment Center installs the EndPoint on them once you know which ones they are.

docs.title: How it works: from target to installed EndPoint
docs.text:
The journey has six steps, and it is worth keeping them in mind because each one leaves a different trace when something fails.

  1. The target is registered. The console stores its address, the access method (SSH, WinRM or Secure WinRM), the port, the credential, the EndPoint version to install, the Tentacle address and port, and a temporary folder. The target knows nothing yet.
  2. A deployment task is created. When you press the deploy button, the console creates a task with the selected target list. The task is enabled and set to a manual interval: it does not repeat on its own, it runs when its turn comes.
  3. The Discovery server runs it. The discovery server takes the task and, for each target, launches the deployment utility. If the Discovery server is remote, it is the one that must reach the targets; the console only gives the order.
  4. The connection is opened. The utility logs in over SSH or WinRM with the stored credential, checks that it can run a command and, if it can, moves on.
  5. The target downloads the installer. Here is the twist: the target opens a TCP connection to the Tentacle, at the configured address and port, and requests the file by name. The Tentacle serves it from the agent directory. It is a download, not a push.
  6. It installs and starts. The installer puts the EndPoint in place, sets the server address, enables remote configuration and starts the service. From then on, the EndPoint reports like any other agent.
flowchart LR
    CONSOLA["Web console<br/>Deployment Center"]
    TAREA["Deployment task"]
    DISCOVERY["Discovery server"]
    OBJETIVO["Target<br/>Linux or Windows"]
    TENTACLE["Tentacle server<br/>EndPoint installers"]
    AGENTE["Installed EndPoint"]

    CONSOLA -->|"creates the task with the targets"| TAREA
    TAREA --> DISCOVERY
    DISCOVERY -->|"SSH 22 or WinRM 5985/5986"| OBJETIVO
    OBJETIVO -->|"requests the installer (pull)"| TENTACLE
    TENTACLE -->|"serves the file"| OBJETIVO
    OBJETIVO -->|"runs the installer"| AGENTE
    AGENTE -->|"reports to the server"| DISCOVERY

The Discovery server processes targets one at a time within the same task. There is no parallel deployment spreading the load across ten machines: there is a queue and one target at a time. There are no automatic retries either. If a target fails, the error is recorded and the next one starts; retrying is your decision, using the task's force button or creating another task. The maximum time per target comes from the repository: the screen proposes 500 seconds and the server stops the run when it is exhausted. A target that hangs does not block the queue forever, but it can take a while to be released.

There is a consequence worth understanding from the start: "deployed" means the installer finished, not that the EndPoint is already reporting. The success mark is set when the deployment utility exits without error; the agent's first contact may arrive seconds or minutes later. Tracking: targets, states and tasks explains how to tell one from the other.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before adding the first target, four things must be ready: access to the machines, the Tentacle server, the credential and the repository. If one is missing, the deployment either does not start or fails at the worst moment.

Requirement Detail SSH access on Linux Port 22 open and password authentication. The utility uses the credential password; it does not support private keys. The user must be able to run the installer as root, because the Linux installer requires it WinRM access on Windows WinRM or Secure WinRM enabled, PowerShell available and a local administrator account. Default ports 5985 (WinRM) and 5986 (Secure WinRM) Reachable Tentacle server The target must be able to open a TCP connection to port 41121 on the Tentacle server. The target starts the connection, not the server Tentacle filters The Tentacle must serve the repository installers. The filters for .agent_setup.tar.gz and .agent_setup.exe in the agent directory are required, and the service must be restarted after changing them Custom credential A credential of type custom with a user name and password, registered in the credential store. Its identifier is what the target stores Repository with installers At least one installer per operating system and architecture, uploaded to the EndPoints repository and synchronised with the server's agent directory PM profile The Deployment Center and its menu entry require the PM profile. The link to the credential store also requires UM Network scanning utility on the Discovery server Only for network scanning. Without it, the scan cannot discover hosts Management network The Discovery server must reach the deployment ports on the targets, and the targets must reach the Tentacle. Opening port 41121 on the server towards the target is useless: the connection goes the other way

The Windows detail is not decoration: WinRM is disabled by default on many installations and, if the network is marked as public, the firewall blocks the port even when the service is running. The WinRM setup guide is still the starting point. In the lab, Windows 11 needed the listener enabled and a firewall rule for the management network; without that, the port appeared closed from the server.

About the Linux user: the installer checks that it runs as root and aborts if not. The utility does not use sudo and does not elevate privileges on its own, so the credential must be root, or an account that already has root privileges in the session. If the machine allows SSH but not root with a password, the Deployment Center is not the way; install by hand or change the access policy.

About Secure WinRM: it uses HTTPS and validates the server certificate. A self-signed or expired certificate will make the connection fail; for a lab it is usually faster to start with WinRM on 5985 and leave Secure WinRM for when the certificate is in order.

Tentacle is not optional

The Deployment Center does not carry the installer inside the SSH or WinRM connection. The target downloads it from the Tentacle. If the target cannot reach the Tentacle, the deployment fails with a connection error even when the credential is correct. This is the most common failure the first time it is tried on a segmented network.

docs.title: The EndPoints repository
docs.text:
The repository is the pantry of the deployment. It is under Configuration → EndPoints repository and stores the installers that are later served to the targets. Each entry is a combination of operating system, architecture and version; there is no "generic" entry that works for everything.

Field What goes in it OS Linux or Windows. These are the two systems the Deployment Center can install Architecture x64 or x86 Version The EndPoint version, up to 10 characters. It is the one shown in the target list and stored as the installed version Transfer timeout Maximum time, in seconds, allowed for downloading and installing that installer. The screen proposes 500 Installation file The EndPoint package. For Linux, a .tar.gz; for Windows, an .exe

On save, the console copies the file to its store and synchronises it with the server's agent directory, which is where the installer is served from. Do not rename files by hand or move them around.

The upload has three decisions that matter:

  • The version cannot be repeated for the same system and architecture. If an entry with that combination already exists, the console rejects the upload. To change it, edit the existing entry (only the transfer timeout) or delete it and upload again.
  • The file type is checked on upload. The console only accepts a .tar.gz for Linux and an .exe for Windows; anything else gets an invalid installation file error.
  • Synchronisation is part of the upload. It is not enough for the file to be in the repository: it must be in the Tentacle's agent directory. The upload does it for you; the refresh icon in the list synchronises an existing entry again if the copy in the agent directory was lost or updated.

Installers come from the same sources described in 1.1 (Installation). The online installer and the repository are not the same thing: the former downloads the package from Pandora FMS servers and installs it on the machine; the latter stores the package you upload so the Deployment Center can serve it over Tentacle. If you upgrade the EndPoint version, upload the new installer to the repository before changing the desired version of the targets.

docs.title: Credentials and permissions
docs.text:
The Deployment Center does not store user names or passwords on the target. It stores the identifier of a credential in the store and retrieves it at deployment time. That indirection has an obvious advantage: when the password for the machines changes, you update it once in the store and the targets use the new one on the next deployment. It also has a consequence: if you delete the credential, the targets that used it can no longer deploy and you must assign another one.

The credential this chapter needs is of type custom: an identifier, a user name and a password. The identifier is what you choose in the target form and what you write in the CSV; the user name and password are not copied to the target. In the store, the credential belongs to a group, and that group decides who can see it. The details of types, groups and encryption are in 2.2 (Credential store).

Credential encryption

If encryption is not enabled, the credential store screen warns that credentials are stored unencrypted. A plaintext password store is a gift to anyone who gets a copy of the data.

As for permissions, the Deployment Center is an administration screen: the menu entry and the page require the PM profile. The link to the credential store only appears with UM; without it, you can use an existing credential but cannot create a new one from there. The group chosen when creating the deployment task decides its visibility in the task list, as with any other Discovery task.

docs.title: Finding targets
docs.text:
There are three ways to fill the target list: scan a network, add one by hand or load a CSV. All three end up in the same place, the target list, and all three store the same information. The difference is how much work you want to do and how much you want the console to do.

Before deploying, it helps to know which targets are valid. The console only offers those with a credential and an EndPoint version in Available targets. A target without a credential, or with a version that no longer exists in the repository, does not appear. It is not a whim: without those two pieces the deployment cannot start.

docs.title: Scanning one or more networks
docs.text:
Scanning is the convenient route when you do not know exactly what is on the network. You give it one or more networks with their mask, a Discovery server, a desired version and one or more credentials, and it does the dirty work: it runs a network sweep, keeps the live hosts and, for each one that is not already a target, tries to connect.

The connection test walks three methods in this order: SSH on 22, WinRM on 5985 and Secure WinRM on 5986. For each method it tries every selected credential. The first combination that manages to run a command is the one stored: the target is added with that method, that port and the corresponding temporary folder. If none works, the host is discarded and the next one starts.

Three details save trouble:

  • The scan does not deploy. It only adds targets to the list. When it finishes, you still have to select them and start the deployment. The scan task appears in the task list with its progress and a summary of live and connected hosts.
  • The scan does not touch existing targets. If a host is already in the list, it skips it. That avoids duplicates, but it also means a target with the wrong credential is not fixed by itself: edit it or delete it and scan again.
  • The first method that works wins. A Windows machine with OpenSSH enabled may accept SSH and end up with the SSH method; the deployment will then use the Linux procedure, which does not work on a Windows machine. If the machines run different systems, check the method the scan chose before deploying.

The scan can take a while. The sweep walks the network, and for each live host it tries three methods per credential; on a large network with several credentials, the task can spend minutes working. Progress is shown in the task list, and the final summary says how many hosts were found and how many accepted the connection.

docs.title: Adding a target manually
docs.text:
Manual entry is for when you already know the address, the method and the credential. It is faster than a scan and more precise: there is no interpretation involved.

Field Meaning Target IP Address of the machine that will receive the EndPoint Deploy method SSH, WinRM or Secure WinRM. When you change the method, the console adjusts the port and the temporary folder to the method's values Deploy port Connection port. 22 for SSH, 5985 for WinRM, 5986 for Secure WinRM. It can be changed if the service listens elsewhere Desired EndPoint version Repository version to install Credentials Custom credential used to access the machine Tentacle server IP Address of the Tentacle server the target will use to download the installer and, later, to report Tentacle server PORT Tentacle port. Defaults to 41121 Deploy temp folder Temporary folder where the installer is downloaded and extracted. /tmp on Linux, C:\Windows\Temp on Windows

The field most often got wrong is Tentacle server IP. The console proposes the address it sees itself, which in a normal installation is the server's address, but in a container or NAT environment it may be an internal address the target cannot reach. Put the address the target can reach, not the one the console thinks it has. If the target is on another network, that address will be the server's interface on that network, not localhost.

The other decision is the temporary folder. On Linux, /tmp usually works; on Windows, C:\Windows\Temp is the default. The installer is downloaded there, run and deleted; if the user cannot write to that folder, the deployment fails before it starts.

The console validates the minimum: that there is an IP, a credential, a version and a protocol. It does not check the IP format or the port range. If the IP already exists, it returns a target-already-defined notice and does not create a duplicate; to change it, edit the existing target.

docs.title: Loading targets from CSV
docs.text:
The CSV is the way to add many targets at once. The format is the one shown on the screen itself:

IP; Protocol; Target port; Target EndPoint version; Credential identifier; Tentacle server ip; Tentacle server port; Temp folder

The separator is chosen in the form: ,, ;, :, . or #; the default is ;. The first line is not a header: every line is processed as a target. If you copy the header above into the file, the console will try to add a target called "IP" and will fail.

Two values are written differently from what they look like:

  • Target EndPoint version is the repository's numeric identifier, not the version string. If the target list shows 8.0.2608 - Linux - x64, the CSV must contain the identifier of that entry (for example, 1), not the text. The console checks that the identifier exists and rejects the line if it does not.
  • Protocol accepts SSH, HTTP or HTTPS. HTTP is WinRM and HTTPS is Secure WinRM; do not write "WinRM" or "Secure WinRM" in the CSV, because the console does not recognise them as protocols.

If the IP already exists, the line updates the target; if it does not, it inserts it. Empty fields are filled from the target's previous value, if it exists, or from the defaults: the deployment port for the protocol, the console server address for the Tentacle, 41121 for the port and /tmp or C:\Windows\Temp for the temporary folder. The final report says how many lines were processed, how many were added and what errors occurred; errors are counted per line, and the whole file is not aborted.

A small CSV first

Before uploading two hundred targets, upload two. Check that the version identifier and the credential identifier are correct and that the separator is the one you chose. A badly separated CSV does not fail in an obvious way: it produces a list of per-line errors that must be read one by one.

docs.title: Deploying the EndPoint
docs.text:
With the targets in the list, deployment is the short step. Press Deploy EndPoint to targets, choose a task name, a group, the Discovery server that will run it and the targets. The console only offers targets with a credential and a version; the rest do not appear in Available targets.

On accept, the console creates a deployment task, enabled, with a manual interval and the chosen group. The task runs in the background. You do not have to watch the screen: you can close it and come back later; progress and results remain in the task list and the target list.

For each target, the utility does the following:

  1. Checks that the target is not already being deployed. If it is, it skips it.
  2. Marks the target as "deploying".
  3. Retrieves the credential.
  4. Finds the installer in the repository.
  5. Prepares the deployment order and launches it with a maximum time.
  6. If the utility exits successfully, marks the target as deployed, stores the installed version and clears the previous error. If it fails, marks the target as not deployed and stores the error output. If time runs out, it stores Deployment timeout after N seconds.

On Linux, the utility downloads the .tar.gz to the temporary folder, extracts it, adjusts the EndPoint configuration and runs the installer unattended. If the machine already had an EndPoint, it keeps its existing configuration and does not rewrite the server address or port. On Windows, it downloads the .exe, stops the service if it already exists, runs it silently with the server address and remote configuration enabled, adds the port if it is not the default and starts the service. If a configuration already exists, it is preserved: a reinstall does not rewrite the server address or the remote-configuration state, and only adds the port if it is not the default. The server address and remote configuration given at deployment time are applied when the EndPoint is installed for the first time.

What “deployed” exactly means

The center marks the target as deployed when the deployment utility exits, not when the EndPoint has already contacted the server. The agent's first contact may arrive seconds or minutes later. If the agent does not appear in the console, check connectivity and the EndPoint log.

In the console, what you see is the agent alias, which defaults to the machine's hostname. If you want to change how it appears, edit the alias.

A reinstall is not a wipe and a clean install. On Linux, if the machine already had an EndPoint, the installer keeps its configuration and does not apply the new Tentacle address. That is good for not losing modules or settings, but it is a trap if you wanted to move the agent to another server: the target will keep pointing to the previous server. To change servers, edit the EndPoint configuration on the machine or uninstall it before deploying again.

docs.title: Tracking: targets, states and tasks
docs.text:
The target list is the deployment dashboard. Each row is a machine, and each entry tells part of its story.

Field What it shows Target IP Target address. If the agent already exists in the console, the IP links to its page Deploy method SSH, WinRM or Secure WinRM Tentacle server IP Address of the Tentacle the target uses Desired EndPoint version Version to install Last EndPoint version deployed Last version installed successfully, with its system and architecture Last successful deployment How long ago the last successful deployment was Last deploy error Output of the last error, if any State Colour indicator with its tooltip Options Edit or delete the target

The state is read by colour and tooltip, not by a label written in the cell. A not deployed target appears in blue; a successfully deployed one in green; a failed one in red. While it is deploying, the last-deployment field shows the text "Deploying" and an unlock icon, and the state stays blue. That icon is the emergency exit: if the process hung, unlocking releases the mark, leaves a note that it was manually unlocked in the error and lets you try again; the row appears as failed until the next successful deployment. It does not cancel the process running on the server; it only releases the mark.

The filters at the top let you search by IP, method, version, Tentacle IP and state. They are useful as the list grows, although the "Deployed" state filter is not reliable on this screen. To know whether a specific target is fine, the state and the last-error fields are more reliable than that filter.

Tasks live in Discovery → Task list → Host & devices tasks. Each deployment appears as a deployment task, with its status, progress and update time.

The task operations are the usual Discovery ones, with nuances:

  • Force runs the task again with the same targets. It is the way to retry a failed deployment without creating a new task.
  • Edit opens the deployment form if the task has targets, or the scan form if it is a network task. It lets you change the name, group, server and targets.
  • Enable/Disable turns the task on or off. A disabled task does not run, but it is not deleted.
  • Delete removes the task. It does not uninstall the EndPoint from the targets or delete the targets from the list; it only removes the task.

If you used the scan to fill the list, the scan task and the deployment task are different. The first only adds targets; the second installs them. Do not mix their results: a successful scan does not mean the EndPoint is installed.

docs.title: Diagnosis and common problems
docs.text:
When a deployment fails, there are three places to look, in this order: the target's last error in the list, the server log and the EndPoint log on the machine itself. The last error usually gives the clue; the server log adds the task context; the EndPoint log says whether the EndPoint managed to start.

Symptom Probable cause What to do The target does not appear in Available targets It is missing the credential or the version; or the credential or version was deleted Edit the target and assign both; check that the version is still in the repository Authentication fails or the connection is refused Wrong user or password, or the method is not the one the machine expects Test the credential by hand over SSH or WinRM; check the method and port No route to host when connecting to the Tentacle The target cannot reach the configured IP or port Fix the Tentacle IP on the target; check port 41121 and the firewall A warning that it could not connect to the Tentacle The Tentacle is down, not listening on that address, or the filter does not serve the file Check the Tentacle service, the address and the installer filters The scan finds the host but does not add it No credential works, or the host already exists with another credential Test the credentials by hand; delete the old target if you want the scan to create it again The CSV rejects a line because the version does not exist The version string was used instead of the repository identifier Use the numeric identifier of the repository entry The CSV rejects a line because the credential does not exist The credential identifier does not match exactly Copy the identifier from the store, with no spaces or case changes The target stays in "Deploying" The process was interrupted or the server did not release the mark Use the target's unlock action and start the deployment again The installation runs out of time The download or installation took longer than the transfer timeout Increase the time in the repository or check the network and the installer size The agent does not appear in the console The EndPoint did not start, cannot reach the server, or the name changed Check the service, the server address and port configured on the EndPoint, connectivity and the EndPoint log

The Tentacle error is the easiest to diagnose and the easiest to avoid. In the lab, a target whose Tentacle IP had been changed to a non-existent address failed with a connection error (No route to host) and a warning that it could not connect to the Tentacle. The credential was correct and the SSH connection worked; what did not work was the return path to the Tentacle. If the error mentions the Tentacle, do not waste time on the password: the problem is the network or the address.

On Linux, the target needs a shell with the usual compression and service-management utilities; on a minimal system the download may fail even when SSH works. On Windows, it needs PowerShell and the EndPoint service; the installer is a silent .exe.

For general server and agent diagnosis, 9.13 (Troubleshooting with Pandora) covers the checks that go beyond this chapter.

docs.title: Security and best practices
docs.text:
The Deployment Center moves credentials, installs software and starts services. It is not a screen to leave open to anyone, and the network it runs on should be treated as a management network.

On the connection side, it helps to know what the Deployment Center does and does not do:

  • SSH accepts whatever host key it finds and does not verify it against a trust list. It uses password authentication, not private keys. On a controlled management network that is acceptable; on an open network, it is a man-in-the-middle risk.
  • WinRM uses NTLM. Secure WinRM adds TLS and validates the server certificate; if the certificate is not trusted, the connection fails. For production, Secure WinRM with a proper certificate is the sensible choice.
  • Tentacle serves installers without a password or encryption by default. Traffic is plaintext. If the network is not trusted, configure the Tentacle security options described in 9.4 (Tentacle reference).
  • Credentials are stored encrypted if encryption is enabled; if not, they are stored in plaintext and the screen warns about it.
  • The temporary folder is used to download and run the installer. The utility deletes the installer when it finishes, but while the deployment lasts the file is there. On a shared machine, use a folder with restricted permissions.

The best practices are those of any mass deployment: test on a pilot target first, do not launch two hundred without having seen one work, keep the repository at the version you want to install, check the method the scan chose and avoid using the same root credential for every machine if you can. The Deployment Center does not force any of that; it only makes it easier if you do it.

docs.title: Relationship with other installation methods
docs.text:
The Deployment Center is one more piece of the puzzle. The choice depends on how many machines there are, whether they have internet access and whether they have already been located.

Method When to use it Where it is explained Online installer One or a few machines with internet access and a known server IP 1.1 (Installation) Manual installation Machines without a management network, without SSH/WinRM or with special requirements 1.1 (Installation) Deployment Center Several machines reachable over SSH/WinRM and a shared Tentacle This chapter Autoprovisioning Machines that register themselves with a predefined configuration 6.6 (Autoprovisioning mechanisms) Discovery with policies Already monitored machines that receive configuration in bulk 2.3 (Monitoring and automatic discovery with Discovery) and 2.10 (Monitoring policies)

The Deployment Center leaves the EndPoint installed. What it reports, with which modules and which alerts, is another conversation: it starts in 2.1 (Monitoring with EndPoints). Installing the agent is the beginning, not the end.

docs.title: Historical database
docs.text: A Pandora FMS installation keeps track of everything: the value of each module, each event, each trap. Over time that database becomes a huge archive, and the part consulted every day is a thin strip, the last few days. The historical database exists for exactly that: old data moves to another database and the main one breathes. The information is not thrown away or locked in a drawer: it stays available, and the console queries it transparently when you ask for a graph or a report that goes back further than the active database keeps.

docs.title: Introduction: what it is and when to use it
docs.text:
The historical database is a second database, with the same engine and the same schema as the main one, to which the server transfers the old data of the modules. The goal is twofold: to lighten the active database, which is the one that supports constant writing and day-to-day queries, and to keep long time series without them taking up the same room as recent data. What is gained is headroom: an installation with a lot of volume can keep storing months of data without the active database degrading. What is paid is one more piece to administer, with its own database server, its own backup and its own maintenance.

It is worth it when there is a high volume of time series and a long history is wanted without sacrificing the response of the main database. The historical database keeps the data as it is, only somewhere else: it does not summarise or lose resolution, and that is why it also serves to look again at the exact minute in which something happened.

It is not a backup either, and it is worth not confusing them. The historical database does not protect against accidental deletion or against a server crash: it is one more production database, alive, with its own purge cycle. That is what the backup is for, and it is covered in 6.9 (Backup y restore).

The historical database is optional and comes disabled from the factory. It is not an installation requirement or a performance lever to be switched on without thinking: it is a piece that gets assembled when the volume justifies it. Enabling it on a small installation adds work in exchange for little. The reasonable decision is to enable it when the active database starts to fall short and the retention needed far exceeds what is convenient to keep in the main database.

If you want to place the historical database within the whole platform before going into detail, 1.2 (Introduction and architecture) describes the components and the topologies, and 10.1 (Database schema) shows the real schema, with the table names that are not used here.

docs.title: How it fits into the architecture
docs.text:
The historical database uses the same engine as the main one, MySQL 8 or Percona Server for MySQL 8. It is not a different store with another format: it is the same structure, with the same data tables, on another server. That is why the server can move rows from one place to another without odd conversions, and why the console can switch sources without the query noticing.

The movement is run by the server's periodic maintenance, not by the Web console. The console only configures the connection and the thresholds; the one that transfers the data is the database maintenance tool, which runs every hour through cron. This has a practical consequence that is sometimes overlooked: configuring the historical database moves nothing instantly. Data starts to travel on the next maintenance pass.

The console, for its part, keeps its own connection to the historical database and decides on each query which database to pull from. When you ask for a graph or a report, the console looks at the age of the requested period and, if it crosses the configured threshold, switches databases. It is the transparent query: you do not choose the database, the console chooses it for you. The detail of that mechanism is in Query from the console.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ACTIVA["Main database"]
        RECIENTES["Recent module data"]
    end
    subgraph HISTORICO["Historical database"]
        ANTIGUOS["Old data already moved"]
    end
    SERVIDOR["Pandora FMS server<br/>hourly maintenance"]
    CONSOLA["Web console"]

    SERVIDOR -->|"moves the data older than the threshold"| HISTORICO
    ACTIVA -->|"maintenance takes the data no longer queried daily"| SERVIDOR
    CONSOLA -->|"1. looks for recent data first"| ACTIVA
    CONSOLA -->|"2. if the period crosses the threshold, queries here"| HISTORICO

The historical database coexists with the rest of the architecture without asking permission. In a Command Center it has its own screen in the Metasetup, as explained in Operation in complex environments; in a high availability topology it is part of the framework that maintenance coordinates, as seen in 6.10 (Alta disponibilidad). And although habit and old documentation present it as mandatory, the truth is that the code does not require the historical database to live on a server different from the main database one: it is a recommendation, and a good one, because separating the disk and the CPU of the two databases keeps the maintenance of one from drowning the other.

docs.title: Requirements and preparation of the historical server
docs.text:
Before touching the console, the server that will host the second database has to be ready. The requirements are the same as those of any Pandora FMS database, with the exception that here the product does not have to be installed: the engine and a dedicated database are enough.

Requirement Detail Database engine MySQL 8 or Percona Server for MySQL 8, the same as the main database. The complete requirements table is in 1.1 (Installation) Dedicated database A database of its own for the historical one, different from the main one, with its own user and password Privileges The user needs privileges on that database, including those to create and modify structure, because the schema is installed on the first connection Connectivity Access from the Pandora FMS server and from the Web console to the host and port of the engine. The default port is 3306 Separate server Hosting the historical database on a server separate from the main database one is recommended, not required. It separates disk and CPU, and keeps the maintenance of one database from penalising the other Secure connection (SSL) Optional since version 782. It is configured with the Enable SSL switch and the key, certificate, CA, CA path and server certificate verification fields

The engine administrator prepares the database and the user. On the command line of the MySQL server that will host the historical database, a set of statements like this one leaves the ground ready:

CREATE USER '<pfms_user_name>' IDENTIFIED BY '<pfms_user_password>';

ALTER USER '<pfms_user_name>'
  IDENTIFIED WITH mysql_native_password BY '<pfms_user_password>';

CREATE DATABASE <historical_database_name>;

GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES
  ON `<historical_database_name>`.*
  TO '<pfms_user_name>'@'<pfms_server_ip_address>';

FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

The database name, the user and the password are the ones written later on the console screen. The schema is not created by hand: the console itself installs it on the first connection, as explained in the following section.

About SSL, it is worth being clear on what each field is. SSL server key is the path to the PEM file with the MySQL server key; SSL server cert, the path to the certificate for that key; SSL CA cert, the list of certificates issued by a certification authority; SSL CA path, the directory that hosts those certificates, also in PEM format. With SSL verify server cert enabled, the connection checks the CN of the certificate and, if it does not match, does not connect. It is the recommended option when the engine exposes a TLS connection, and the explanation of the secure configuration of the main database, which shares criteria, is in 9.5 (Database encryption).

docs.title: Enabling and connecting from the console
docs.text:
The screen lives in Settings → System settings → Historical database. Everything starts with a general switch, Enable historical database, and a connection form that appears when it is enabled.

The connection fields are those of any MySQL client: Host, Port, Database name, Database user and Database password. The port comes with 3306, the standard one. The password is stored encrypted, like the rest of the product credentials. Below is the SSL block described in the previous section.

On saving, the console runs two checks that are worth knowing because they explain half of the scares:

  • If the historical database you have typed is the same as the active one (same host, same port, same name), the console rejects the save with a clear warning: the active database and the historical one cannot be the same. It is a configuration error, not a failure.
  • If the destination database does not exist, does not respond or the user has no permissions, the creation of the structure fails and the Enable historical database switch is left disabled. The console does not leave a historical database enabled that it cannot write to.

When the connection is fine, the first time the schema is installed in the destination database. From then on, the console compares the schema version of the historical database with that of the active database and offers two actions depending on the state: Install database schema, if it does not exist yet, and Upgrade database schema, which schedules the update when the historical database has fallen behind the main one. Both actions are the same machinery that keeps the schema of the main database up to date, applied to the historical connection.

The status indicators of the Connection tab are not decorative: they can be clicked to force a check. If you doubt whether the database responds, clicking the connection indicator launches a check right away, without waiting for the next cycle. The installed schema indicator is the one that triggers the installation when it is missing, and the updated schema one the one that schedules the upgrade when there is a mismatch.

The screen is organised into five tabs, each with its own purpose:

Tab What it configures Connection The general switch, the connection data, the SSL block and the status of maintenance and of the schema Active to historical What data leaves the active database and with what age, the block size, the pause and the advanced options Historical data The retention of the data already moved and the automatic partitioning of large tables Historical events The transfer of events and their retention in the historical database Historical traps The transfer of traps and their retention in the historical database. It does not appear in the Command Center

The complete inventory of options, with their default value and their effect, lives in 9.2 (Full console configuration reference). Here the chapter covers what each thing does and how it is operated.

docs.title: What moves and when
docs.text:
The first thing the historical database moves is the numeric series of the modules. From a threshold of age, 15 days by default, the data stops being in the active database and goes to the historical one. The threshold is set in Data days old to keep in active database and cannot reach the purge limit of the main database: if the active database deletes at 45 days, the historical database makes no sense configured at 45, because it would arrive late to collect what has already been purged.

Text series are another story. By default they are not transferred: they stay in the active database and are purged with it. They only leave for the historical database if the Advanced options are enabled, which enable the field String data days old to keep in active database, with 0 days by default: strings do not wait in the active database and start travelling to the historical one as soon as they are enabled. It is a decision with consequences, because text strings take up much more than a number and, if they are enabled, their purging has to be configured in the historical database or it will grow unchecked. That point is covered in Retention and purging.

Events and traps are optional and travel through switches of their own: Enable historical events and Enable historical traps. Each one has its own age threshold in the active database. The events one, Events days old to keep in active database, has 6 days by default, one day below the event purging of the main database (7). The traps one, in its tab, is 6 days by default. Besides, events are queried only when generating reports, never in the live event view, so taking them to the historical database fattens the second database without speeding up the screen that is watched the most: including events notably increases the growth rate of the historical database, and it is a space decision, not a performance one.

There is a separate case that explains more than one surprise: short-interval modules. Those that run with an interval under 300 seconds live in the active database for a maximum of one week, and that term is fixed: it is hard-coded and is not configured from the console. After the week, their data move to the historical database. The reason is common sense: a module that measures every few seconds generates a huge volume, and leaving it in the active database for months is the fastest way to bring it down. This behaviour coexists with the general threshold of 15 days, which applies to normal-interval modules.

The transfer is not done all at once. Maintenance sends the data in blocks whose size is set by Transference block size (Step), 1500 rows by default, and waits Delay between transferences (seconds), 1 second by default, between one block and the next. The idea is not to eat the active database while it is being emptied: small blocks and generous pauses disturb less, at the cost of taking longer to complete the transfer. If maintenance gives problems, the help of the field itself recommends lowering the block size. The recommended values are revisited in Options reference and sizing.

All this coming and going is done by the periodic maintenance. If you want to understand which modules generate what volume before deciding the thresholds, 2.1 (Monitoring with EndPoints) covers the module intervals, and 10.1 (Database schema) shows the detail of what moves at table level.

docs.title: Retention and purging
docs.text:
The historical database has its own purge cycle, with its own limits. It does not inherit those of the main database: the fact that the active database keeps 45 days of numeric data means nothing for the historical database, which decides on its own how much it keeps. The default limits are 180 days for numeric data, 180 for text strings, 180 for events and 180 for traps. They are set in the data, events and traps tabs of the historical database.

Meanwhile, the main database purges at the same time on its own, with much shorter limits: 45 days of numeric data, 7 of strings, 7 of events and 7 of traps. Order matters. On each pass, maintenance first purges from the active database what exceeds its retention limit and then moves to the historical database what exceeds the transfer threshold. That is why the transfer threshold should always stay below the purge limit: if the active database deletes before the historical one collects, the data is lost. And if the historical database is not available, the active database keeps purging all the same: there is no waiting queue. That is why the status of the historical database, seen on the Connection tab, deserves a look from time to time.

The serious warning is the one about text series. If the advanced options are enabled to transfer them, their retention in the historical database has to be configured too. If that is not done, strings pile up in the second database indefinitely and end up taking space nobody had foreseen. Old documentation proposed solving it with a direct SQL query on the database; here the recommendation is to do it from the screen itself, which is what it is for, and to leave the detail of tables and columns to 10.1 (Database schema).

docs.title: Automatic partitioning of large tables
docs.text:
With the historical database full of series, the largest tables become slow to query and heavy to purge. Automatic partitioning of large tables spreads those tables into monthly partitions, so that a query for a graph or a report touches only the pieces of the period it is interested in and purging works on smaller row sets instead of on the whole table.

The switch is on the Historical data tab, under the name Automatic partition of big tables., and it comes disabled by default. When it is enabled, maintenance creates the missing partitions and adds a new one at the start of each month. It covers three families of data: numeric series, text series and traps. The rest of the database is not partitioned. The detail of the schema and of the table names involved is in 10.1 (Database schema) and in 10.2 (Table reference).

There is also manual partitioning, for those who prefer to control the process or do not want to depend on the automation. The operation is done with an ALTER TABLE on the series table, declaring partitions by range on the timestamp, with a final partition that collects everything above the last limit:

ALTER TABLE <series_table>
  PARTITION BY RANGE (<timestamp>) (
    PARTITION <month_1> VALUES LESS THAN (UNIX_TIMESTAMP('<start_of_month_2>')),
    PARTITION <month_2> VALUES LESS THAN (UNIX_TIMESTAMP('<start_of_month_3>')),
    /* ... one stretch per month ... */
    PARTITION pActual VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
  );

Every month the open partition has to be reorganised to close the month that ends and open the next one, with an equivalent REORGANIZE PARTITION. Two warnings from experience: the operation needs plenty of free space on disk, because MySQL rewrites the table while it partitions it, and it can take hours on large tables; in a real case, partitioning a table with tens of millions of rows took about an hour and a half. The way to follow the progress is to look at the partition files the engine creates in the data directory. Manual partitioning rests on the same optimisation ideas covered in 6.8 (Database optimization).

docs.title: Status, maintenance and diagnosis
docs.text:
The Connection tab is the control panel of the historical database, and it is worth reading in order. First, the connection availability: a green indicator with "History database connection is available" or a red one with the specific error. Second, the installed schema: whether it exists, or whether it is missing and has to be installed. Third, the schema up to date: whether the version of the historical database matches that of the active database or has fallen behind. And finally, the current schema version of the historical database, to compare it at a glance with that of the main database.

The maintenance status of each database, active and historical, is followed from the Performance page of the console, in its maintenance block. Each row says when maintenance last ran and shows a warning if too much time has passed. In practice, the reference is 12 hours: if maintenance has not run within that term, the indicator goes to a problematic state. Since maintenance is scheduled every hour, twelve hours without running mean something is wrong.

On top of that come the warnings of the console supervisor, which appear in the notification system and cover three cases:

  • Historical database not available. The historical database is enabled but the console cannot connect with the current configuration.
  • Historical database maintenance problem. Maintenance does not go through the database in 48 hours. It is the threshold of the supervisor, more lenient than the indicator on the screen, and it warns of sustained neglect.
  • Historical database MR mismatch. The historical database does not use the same schema as the main database, something that can produce anomalies when storing data.

When maintenance has to be checked by hand, the tool is launched from the command line:

/usr/bin/pandora_db /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf

A correct run should report no errors. The process leaves its trace in the server error file, which by default is /var/log/pandora/pandora_server.error and is configured in the server file itself.

If something still does not add up, the general diagnosis of the product is in 9.13 (Troubleshooting) and the server and database frequently asked questions, in 12.2 (Servidor y base de datos) and 12.8 (Entornos grandes).

docs.title: Query from the console
docs.text:
The beauty of the historical database is that there is no need to remember it. When you ask for a graph or a report with old data, the console looks first in the main database and, as soon as the requested period crosses the configured age threshold, switches to the historical database and keeps pulling from there. The query is split between the two databases without the user noticing, and the result appears as a continuous series. That threshold is the same 15 days by default that decides what moves, so that what is no longer in the active database is looked for where it is.

Reports benefit from the transparency in the same way, as described in 5.2 (Informes), and business and service views, in 5.3 (Monitorización de negocio y servicios).

It is also worth knowing what the historical database does not cover. The live event view does not query the historical database: the events moved only feed report generation. If you transfer events, you gain history for reports, but you will not see the old events on the events screen. Something similar happens with traps, whose treatment is documented in 2.7 (SNMP trap monitoring). And there is data that never travels to the historical database: configuration, agents, alerts and everything that is not a time series stay in the main database.

docs.title: Operation in complex environments
docs.text:
In a Command Center, the historical database has its own screen in Setup → Metasetup → Historical database: it is the same configuration as that of a console, applied to the database of the Command Center itself, and each instance also keeps its own in its console. A practical detail: the connection data can be filled in even if the server is not up yet, and the data movement only starts when the connection succeeds. However, if on saving the connection does not respond, the console disables the switch of the historical database: it has to be enabled again when the destination is available. The traps tab does not appear in the Command Center.

The Command Center as a whole, with its nodes and its management model, is developed in 6.3 (Command Center). Here it is enough to remember that the historical database of the Command Center is configured in its own Metasetup.

In high availability, the historical database is part of the topology and maintenance is coordinated between nodes so that they do not step on each other. The complete scenario, with its precautions, is in 6.10 (Alta disponibilidad).

In a node migration there is a step that is easily forgotten: repointing the historical connection to the new server. The main database moves with its procedure, but the historical one has its own connection configuration and it has to be updated so that the node keeps finding it.

And in the backup it is worth being clear: the copy of the main database does not include the historical database. They are two different databases on two different servers, and each one needs its own backup. The Pandora FMS copy and restore procedure is documented in 6.9 (Backup y restore).

docs.title: Options reference and sizing
docs.text:
This chapter does not repeat the inventory of options or the sizing table, and it does so on purpose. The complete listing of each field of the screen, with its default value and its effect, is in 9.2 (Full console configuration reference). The calculation of how much the database will grow according to agents and modules, and how to distribute storage, is in 9.14 (Análisis de volumetría y diseños para alta capacidad). Here only the operating criteria remain.

About how many days to keep in the active database, the short answer is the fewest that allow working comfortably with day-to-day data. The default value, 15 days, is a good starting point: it gives margin to look at the current month without dragging an unnecessary volume. Lowering it too much forces the console to jump to the historical database too early; raising it too much fattens the database that is written the most.

About the block size and the pause, the code brings 1500 rows and 1 second by default, but the operating recommendation is more conservative: 1000 rows per block and 2 seconds of pause. Smaller blocks and longer pauses spread the load better and keep the transfer from competing with the normal work of the active database. On installations with fast disks the block can go up; on tight installations, lowering it is the first lever when maintenance is rushed.

And about the retention of the historical database, the decision is set by how far back you really need to query. The 180 days by default cover half a year, which is more than most reports require. Extending it has a direct cost in space and in purge time; shortening it frees room. If you enable text series, remember that their retention has to be configured explicitly or they will grow without control, as warned in Retention and purging. To adjust the number with the real growth of the database, the reference is 9.14 (Análisis de volumetría y diseños para alta capacidad), and for the rest of the optimisation techniques, 6.8 (Database optimization).
