docs.title: Introduction: why the database degrades
docs.text:
In a Pandora FMS installation writing never stops: modules deliver their data, events pile up and traps keep arriving. The time series tables grow without pause, periodic maintenance purges the old data, and the space it frees is not always reused well. The result, after a few months, is a database full of holes inside. Graph and report queries, the ones that read the most, slow down, and one day the screen takes a while to paint what it used to paint on its own.

That is degradation, and it is worth being clear from the start about what can be done and what cannot. Pandora FMS does not optimize the database for you. Its periodic maintenance, which runs every hour through cron, does four things: it purges the data that exceeds its retention, it checks the consistency of the database, it reviews its referential integrity and, if a historical database is configured, it moves the old data there. When it finishes, it stamps the time of its last pass. What it does not do is defragment or rebuild anything: there is no hidden OPTIMIZE TABLE in maintenance, and the Web console has no "Optimize" button. If you came here looking for that button, I will save you the search: it does not exist.

Hence the approach of this chapter. What is explained here is not a feature of the product, but the administration of the engine, MySQL or Percona Server for MySQL. You tune the engine, you measure fragmentation, you decide when to optimize and when to rebuild. Pandora FMS gives you the diagnosis and the documentation to do it with judgement.

The rest of the pieces of the puzzle live in other chapters and are not repeated here. The historical database, its retention and the automatic partitioning of its tables are in 6.5 (Historical database). The backup and the restore, which is where the rebuild ends up, in 6.9 (Backup y restore). And the sizing of the system, with how much memory and how much CPU each scenario asks for, in 9.14 (Análisis de volumetría y diseños para alta capacidad).

docs.title: What engine configuration Pandora FMS ships with
docs.text:
Pandora FMS runs on MySQL 8 and its recommended variant, Percona Server for MySQL 8. Both are compatible with each other and, for convenience, this chapter says "MySQL" plainly; wherever a test or a recommended value is mentioned, it was done on Percona.

The first thing worth knowing is that you do not start from scratch. The Pandora FMS installer does not limit itself to leaving the engine with the factory values: it writes a my.cnf with a block of parameters already designed for the product. That block sets, among others, these values:

Parameter Value Parameter Value max_allowed_packet 64M innodb_lock_wait_timeout 90 innodb_file_per_table Enabled innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit 0 innodb_flush_method O_DIRECT innodb_log_buffer_size 16M innodb_log_file_size 512M innodb_io_capacity 1000 thread_cache_size 32 thread_stack 256K max_connections 300 key_buffer_size 4M sql_mode Empty character-set-server utf8mb4 read_buffer_size 128K read_rnd_buffer_size 128K sort_buffer_size 1M join_buffer_size 4M

The last two rows are per-session buffers, not global ones: they are reserved for each connection. The engine uses utf8mb4 on all systems, because it is the default value of MySQL 8, and the dedicated database installer for Ubuntu 22.04 also sets it explicitly in the file. And the block disables binary logs with skip-log-bin, something that is only correct on a single server, as seen in Disk, binary logs and system load.

Four of those values are not fixed. The installer adapts them to the system and to whether the database runs on the same server or on a dedicated one, and they move between two profiles: innodb_log_file_size between 64M and 512M, innodb_io_capacity between 100 and 1000, thread_cache_size between 8 and 32, and max_connections between 100 and 300. On the most recent systems, and above all when the engine is MySQL 8.4, the installer also adds two parameters that do not appear on the others: innodb_change_buffering = ALL and performance_schema = OFF. As the exact value depends on your case, do not trust the table: check the one the running engine has, which is exactly what is explained a little further down.

The InnoDB buffer is the only one without a fixed value: the installer calculates it from the memory of the server. The general rule is 40 % of the RAM, and in several combinations of system and installer it drops to 25 % when the server has less than 7.5 GB. The idea is that it eats a generous portion of the memory and leaves the rest for the system and for the Pandora FMS server. It is the most important decision of the whole engine configuration and it is explained in detail in Fine tuning of the engine parameters.

How to know which configuration is active.

The configuration file is not always where you believe it is, so the fastest way is to ask the engine itself. The server binary prints, with --verbose, the list of files it reads and in what order:

mysqld --help --verbose | head -40

With that you locate the my.cnf that is really being applied (on Ubuntu it is usually /etc/mysql/my.cnf; on the distributions of the RHEL family, /etc/my.cnf). To see the values hot, without opening the file, the engine variables are queried:

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb%';

And for a specific parameter, the same query narrowed to the name:

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_buffer_pool_size';

Parameters must be inside their section

A parameter written outside the [mysqld] section of my.cnf is not applied, and the engine starts up quite happily with the previous value. It is the most common mistake and the hardest one to see, because it gives no warning at all: the value simply does not change. Always check the hot value with SHOW VARIABLES, do not trust the file.

The requirements of the database server, with the operating system and the versions admitted, are in 1.1 (Installation). The my.cnf used by a high availability environment is not this one, but the replication one, which is described in 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)). And if what you are looking for is how much machine is needed for a specific volume, that is 9.14 (Análisis de volumetría y diseños para alta capacidad).

docs.title: Fine tuning of the engine parameters
docs.text:
Here is the bulk of the administration work. The following table gathers the parameters that matter, with the value Pandora FMS applies and what each one is for. Those with a fixed value are the ones the installer writes; those that depend on the system are marked as such.

Parameter Value Pandora FMS applies What it is for innodb_buffer_pool_size Computed: 25 % or 40 % of the RAM, depending on the system In-memory cache of InnoDB data and indexes. It is, by far, the parameter that weighs the most on performance innodb_log_file_size 64M or 512M, depending on the system Size of each InnoDB log file innodb_log_buffer_size 16M In-memory buffer where InnoDB accumulates writes to the log before flushing them to disk innodb_io_capacity 100, 300 or 1000, depending on the system Input/output capacity InnoDB can request from the disk innodb_file_per_table Enabled One tablespace per table, instead of a shared one innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit 0 Write policy on committing each transaction innodb_flush_method O_DIRECT How InnoDB writes to disk, without going through the operating system cache innodb_lock_wait_timeout 90 Seconds a transaction waits for a lock before giving up innodb_thread_concurrency 0 (engine default value) Limit of concurrent InnoDB threads; 0 means "no limit" max_allowed_packet 64M Maximum size of a data packet between client and engine max_connections 100 or 300, depending on the system Simultaneous connections admitted thread_cache_size 8 or 32, depending on the system Threads the engine keeps in reserve to reuse them thread_stack 256K Memory stack assigned to each thread key_buffer_size 4M Key buffer, specific to MyISAM. It does not speed up InnoDB read_buffer_size 128K Per-session buffer for sequential reads read_rnd_buffer_size 128K Per-session buffer for reads in scattered order sort_buffer_size 1M Per-session buffer for sorts join_buffer_size 4M Per-session buffer for joins that do not use an index sql_mode Empty Strict SQL mode disabled

The InnoDB buffer: more memory before more CPU.

If you can only touch one parameter, touch this one. innodb_buffer_pool_size is the memory where InnoDB caches the data and index pages it reads, and the bigger it is, the fewer times it has to go to disk. In a monitoring database, where the pattern is to read a lot and write constantly, this marks the difference between a Web console that responds and one that crawls.

Experience with the product always points in the same direction: more memory delivers more than more CPU. A business system starts fine with 4 GB of RAM; for a large environment, 16 GB is a reasonable starting point. The installer already calculates the value from the available memory, but on large machines it is worth reviewing it, because percentages are an approximation and the number that really matters is how much space the active data and indexes take up. If the buffer fits entirely in memory, the disk stops being the bottleneck for reads.

InnoDB logs and disk capacity.

InnoDB writes its changes to a log before consolidating them in the tables. The installer sets each log file to 64M or 512M, depending on the system, and its buffer to 16M. A small log forces the engine to flush it to disk more often, and that is where performance is lost; a large one lengthens recovery after a crash, because there is more to redo. The Pandora FMS values are a compromise designed for production with a high volume of transactions.

innodb_io_capacity says how much input/output InnoDB can request from the disk. The installer leaves it at a prudent value (between 100 and 1000, depending on the system) that assumes a capable disk. If the disk is different, the number is adjusted to what it can take. The reference is the IOPS of the disk:

Disk type Approximate IOPS Mechanical disk at 7,500 RPM 100 Mechanical disk at 15,000 RPM 190 SSD 1,500

An SSD is not a luxury on a monitoring database server: it is the difference between a maintenance that finishes on time and one that overlaps with the next.

innodb_file_per_table deserves a paragraph of its own because it conditions everything else. With the tablespace per table enabled, each table lives in its own file. That allows moving a specific table to another disk, restoring it without touching the others and, above all, keeping the fragmentation of one table from dragging the others along. If the parameter is not enabled, all tables share a single tablespace and fragmentation is common, so performance degrades sooner. The installer enables it by default, and the manual partitioning of large tables requires it.

The write policy on commit.

innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit decides how much the engine risks in order to go faster. With the value 0, InnoDB groups the writes and flushes them approximately once per second, instead of going to disk on every transaction. The trade-off is clear: in the event of a crash, the last second of data can be lost. In a monitoring database that second is a handful of module values, and the exchange pays off. Pandora FMS applies 0 in the installer; a high availability environment uses another value, because there replication changes the rules of the game and the my.cnf is another one.

Closely related is innodb_flush_method = O_DIRECT, which keeps the writes from going through the operating system cache. In a database that already has a large buffer of its own, duplicating the cache in the system does not help, it gets in the way.

Locks, packets and concurrency.

innodb_lock_wait_timeout sets at 90 seconds the maximum wait of a transaction for a lock. If that time runs out, the operation fails and the client receives the classic "MySQL has gone away". The 90 seconds give margin for an occasional jam to clear itself, without the engine giving up at the first attempt. A wait time that runs out regularly is not a missing setting: it is a symptom that something else is wrong.

max_allowed_packet at 64M allows moving large packets, such as the bulk data sends of the EndPoints or a restore. max_connections (at 100 or 300, depending on the system) covers with room to spare the connections of the console, the server and maintenance, each one with its small group of connections. thread_cache_size and thread_stack complete the thread section: the engine keeps threads in reserve (8 or 32, depending on the system) so as not to create and destroy them on every connection, and assigns 256K of stack to each one.

About innodb_thread_concurrency, the default value 0 lets InnoDB open as many threads as it can. It is an advanced parameter and, badly adjusted, it goes slower than leaving it alone. If it has to be fine-tuned on a system with a lot of concurrency, the recommended formula is the number of physical processors multiplied by two, plus the number of disks where InnoDB lives. When in doubt, it is left at 0.

The per-session buffers.

The four per-session buffers (read_buffer_size, read_rnd_buffer_size, sort_buffer_size and join_buffer_size) are reserved per connection, not once. They are multiplied by the number of simultaneous connections, so raising them cheerfully fattens the memory consumption. The Pandora FMS values are restrained and sufficient for the queries of the product. key_buffer_size, at 4M, is a MyISAM buffer and does not speed up InnoDB; it is kept at its low value because it adds nothing to the engine the product uses.

What no longer exists: the query cache.

MySQL 8 removed the query cache that previous versions brought. The parameters that governed it (query_cache_size, query_cache_limit, query_cache_type) no longer exist, and the Pandora FMS my.cnf does not define them. There is nothing to configure here: if you come from an old installation and those parameters are still in the file, remove them, because the current engine does not recognise them and may refuse to start. They are taken out of my.cnf and you move on.

Every change requires a restart and a check

Engine parameters are not applied hot: the service has to be restarted and you have to verify that it starts without errors and that the Web console and the server still connect to the database. A my.cnf with a syntax error or an out-of-range value can leave the engine down. Change one block, restart, check, and only then move on to the next one.

docs.title: Disk, binary logs and system load
docs.text:
The usual bottleneck of a database is not the CPU or the memory: it is the disk. Three golden rules, and none of them is negotiable when the volume presses. The first, separate the operating system, the database data and the replication logs on different disks, so that they do not compete for the same head or the same controller. The second, use SSD. The third, when the client and the engine are on the same machine, connect through a socket instead of TCP/IP, which translates into an improvement of around 7.5 % without touching anything else: it is enough not to indicate a host name when connecting, instead of forcing localhost.

Binary logs are the other piece of the disk. If you have a single Pandora FMS server, you do not need them and the installer already disables them with skip-log-bin. If you have high availability, they are mandatory, because replication rests on them, and the my.cnf is another one: it carries a block of replication parameters and, besides, a different value for the write policy (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2) and a connection limit of its own (200). That file, with its nodes and its precautions, is documented in 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)).

How to know if the system is suffering.

Before touching the database it is worth checking that the problem is where you think it is. The operating system brings the tool that is needed:

vmstat 1 10

It returns ten samples, one per second. What to watch is in the last columns. An output from a healthy system looks like this:

procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- --system-- -----cpu------
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 0  0  46248  78664 154644 576800    0    0     2   147    0    9  7 10 83  0  0
 2  0  46248  78904 154648 576740    0    0     0   184  728 2484 63  6 31  0  0
 0  0  46248  79028 154648 576736    0    0     0    20   35   37  0  1 98  1  0
 1  0  46248  79028 154648 576736    0    0     0     0   28   22  0  0 100  0  0

The reading is direct. The wa column (input/output wait) above 10 points to a disk problem that has to be solved. The sy column (system time) should not exceed 10 or 15. And si and so (swap memory) should be at 0: if they are not, the system is using swap, which is a performance killer, plain and simple. The solution, then, is not in the database: memory has to be increased or what consumes it has to be reduced, starting with the server threads and the engine buffers.

docs.title: Diagnosing the health of the database
docs.text:
Before optimizing anything, measure. The Web console offers no optimize action, but it does offer a complete diagnosis of the database, and it is worth knowing because it is the gateway to everything else.

The main tool is in Admin tools → Diagnostic info. It gathers, on a single screen, the size of the database, its health status, engine information and two blocks that are the ones of interest here:

  • The engine variables compared with the recommended values. The diagnosis goes through the MySQL variables and marks in red those that do not reach the advised minimum, with their current value and the value they should have. The following table gathers those minimums.
Variable Value recommended by the diagnosis innodb_buffer_pool_size 250 MB or more (the warning itself mentions 40 % of the server memory) innodb_file_per_table Enabled innodb_lock_wait_timeout 90 seconds or more innodb_log_buffer_size 16M or more innodb_log_file_size 64M or more max_allowed_packet 32M or more max_connections 90 or more read_buffer_size 32K or more read_rnd_buffer_size 32K or more sort_buffer_size 32K or more thread_cache_size 8 or more thread_stack 256K or more sql_mode Empty

Besides those minimums, the diagnosis compares each variable with the value it expects to find, including the write policy of InnoDB. If a variable appears in red, review the my.cnf: the usual thing is that the parameter has not been applied because it is outside its section, or that someone changed it later.

There is one row that can come out red and that must not be touched: the one of the InnoDB write policy. The diagnosis expects the conservative value, and the installer of a single server applies the fast one, so in a freshly made installation that row appears in red even though nothing is wrong. Leave it as it is, with the value the installer put. In a high availability environment you will not see it that way: there the my.cnf uses the conservative value and the row comes out green, as told in Disk, binary logs and system load.

  • The fragmentation of the numeric series table. When it exceeds 10 %, the diagnosis warns that the table is fragmented and should be defragmented. It is measured on the same panel and it is explained in Fragmentation: measure it before touching anything.

The other two tools in the menu have a different role. Admin tools → DB Schema Check verifies that the database is correct: it detects tables or fields that are missing after a migration or an update. To run it, the database user needs query, delete, create and references privileges. And Admin tools → DB interface allows launching queries directly against the database from the console, useful for a one-off check without opening a separate client. The general diagnosis of the product, beyond the database, is covered in 9.13 (Troubleshooting con Pandora).

The server diagnostic script.

When an incident has to be opened, the console is not enough: a snapshot of the server is needed. That is what the diagnostic script is for, and it is run by hand on the machine:

./pandora_diagnostic.sh

It gathers, in a single file in /tmp/pandora_diag.<date>.data, processor and memory information, uptime, the Pandora FMS processes running, the contents of the engine my.cnf, the server configuration (without passwords), the listing of its logs, disk usage and a sample of vmstat and of the system log. It is the first piece requested when opening a ticket, because it saves twenty questions. It runs on the server, not from the console, and its result is not read on screen: it is a file that gets attached.

The status of periodic maintenance.

Finally, the status of the database maintenance is monitored from Settings → System settings → Performance, on the database maintenance tab. That screen closes the diagnosis at the bottom: each row says when it last ran and shows a traffic light, so at a glance you know whether the database is being purged and checked at the expected rate or whether maintenance has stopped. The detail of the indicator and of its threshold is in 6.5 (Historical database), and the complete inventory of options of that screen, with their default value, in 9.2 (Full console configuration reference).

docs.title: Fragmentation: measure it before touching anything
docs.text:
A database fragments the way a disk fragments: between one insert and the next there are deletes, and the space left free is spread out in holes. In Pandora FMS the pattern is clear: the time series tables receive constant inserts and the purge deletes old series continuously, so those tables are the first to accumulate unused free space. Over time, reading a graph forces the engine to jump between holes and everything goes slower.

Measuring fragmentation is cheap and changes nothing, so it is always done before deciding. The query goes to the catalogue of the engine itself, not to the tables of the product, and that is why it can be published in full:

SELECT ENGINE,
       TABLE_NAME,
       ROUND(DATA_LENGTH/1024/1024)  AS data_length,
       ROUND(INDEX_LENGTH/1024/1024) AS index_length,
       ROUND(DATA_FREE/1024/1024)    AS data_free,
       (DATA_FREE/(INDEX_LENGTH+DATA_LENGTH)) AS frag_ratio
  FROM information_schema.tables
 WHERE TABLE_TYPE = 'BASE TABLE'
   AND DATA_FREE > 0
 ORDER BY frag_ratio DESC;

Each row is a table with free space and each column measures one thing: the engine (ENGINE), the name of the table (TABLE_NAME), the megabytes of data (data_length), those of indexes (index_length), those of free space (data_free) and the quotient between the free space and the occupied one (frag_ratio). The result comes sorted from most to least fragmented, so the first rows are the candidates.

Two warnings to read it well. The first, that the quotient deceives on small tables: a tiny table with a few free megabytes can give a very high frag_ratio without it mattering to anyone. The quotient and the absolute sizes always have to be looked at, and keep the large tables that also have a high quotient. The second, that the 10 % does not come from the query: it is the threshold the Web console diagnosis applies to the numeric series table, as seen in Diagnosing the health of the database. The query gives you the map; the threshold is set by judgement.

Measuring is only measuring

The query does not touch the data, but on a loaded server and with huge tables it can take a while, because it forces the engine catalogue to be read. Launch it at a quiet moment. And do not expect measuring to fix anything: the fragmentation is still there until the table is optimized.

The detail of which tables are in the schema and what they are called is in 10.1 (Database schema) and in 10.2 (Table reference). Here, and throughout the chapter, tables are described by their role, not by their name.

docs.title: Table optimization
docs.text:
The operation that recovers the space is OPTIMIZE TABLE. It is run on the tables that need it, and the command, with the table name referred to the reference of Part 10, is this one:

OPTIMIZE TABLE <table>;

It is worth optimizing the tables that grow and are purged without pause: the time series tables (the numeric ones and the text series one), the events table, the module inventory table and those of agents, modules and module status. The concrete list of names, with their content and their usual size, is in 10.2 (Table reference). When you finish the batch, it is worth refreshing the engine with:

FLUSH TABLES;

In InnoDB, OPTIMIZE TABLE is not a magic operation: the engine translates it into a rebuild of the table, which updates the index statistics and frees the unused space of the clustered index. That is what the MySQL manual itself says, and it explains both its usefulness and its cost. The engine usually answers with a message that confirms the translation: "Table does not support optimize, doing recreate + analyze instead". It is not an error; it is the way InnoDB has of saying that it is going to rebuild.

And there is the problem. Rebuilding a table means rewriting it entirely, so the operation locks the table and needs, besides, enough free space on disk to host the copy while it is done. If the disk is full, the command fails and does not run. If the table is very large, the rebuild can take hours and get stuck; at that point it stops being an alternative and the right move is rebuilding the database, as explained in Rebuilding the database.

The cadence is not set by the product, it is set by judgement. A normal environment is optimized once a year; a large one, every six months. And always in a maintenance window, because during the operation the table is not available. For the backup and restore procedure, in case something goes wrong, go to 6.9 (Backup y restore).

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
The queries a Pandora FMS installation suffers the most are those of graphs and reports, and almost all of them filter by a module and by a time range. So that those queries do not walk the whole table, the time series tables carry two indexes: one composed of the module and the timestamp, and another one by the timestamp alone. The first resolves the typical query of a module graph; the second covers the sweeps by period.

For years the documentation presented these indexes as "optional", something that had to be added by hand after installing. That is no longer true: the current schema brings them from the factory. If you come across an old installation where they are missing, it is not that they are disabled: it is that the schema is incomplete, and they have to be added.

To check that they are there, there are two paths. The first, the schema check of the Web console, Admin tools → DB Schema Check, which warns of what is missing.

The second, ask the engine for the indexes of a specific table:

SHOW INDEX FROM <table>;

The output returns one row for each column that makes up each index, with its name, its position inside the index and its uniqueness. It is enough to check that the two expected indexes appear: the composite one and the timestamp one. The name of the specific table to query is in 10.2 (Table reference).

If they are missing, they are added with a statement like this one, replacing the placeholders with the real name of the table and of its columns, which are also in the reference:

ALTER TABLE <table>
  ADD INDEX <index_name> (<module_column>, <timestamp_column>);

An index added on a live system does not go unnoticed

Creating an index on a large table locks and consumes resources, and on a production installation it is felt. Do it in a maintenance window, with a recent backup, and check afterwards with SHOW INDEX that the index was created. For the general diagnosis of incidents, 9.13 (Troubleshooting con Pandora).

docs.title: Slow queries
docs.text:
The engine can log the queries that take longer than a threshold, and that log is an excellent diagnostic tool. It is also a tool you pay for, because every query that gets recorded writes to disk and competes with the normal work. The Pandora FMS recommendation is blunt: do not leave it enabled permanently. It is switched on when there is a problem, you look at what you need and it is switched off.

It is enabled in the my.cnf, adding these lines:

slow_query_log = 1
long_query_time = 2
slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql_slow.log

The long_query_time threshold is in seconds: with 2, every query that takes more than two seconds is logged. Before starting, the file has to be created and given the right permissions, because the engine writes to it with its own user:

touch /var/log/mysql_slow.log
chown mysql:mysql /var/log/mysql_slow.log
chmod 640 /var/log/mysql_slow.log

Afterwards, MySQL is restarted and left to work for a while. When you have gathered enough samples, the file is read and the patterns are looked for: queries that repeat, filters that do not make use of an index, sorts that could be avoided. From there come two possible actions, adding an index that is missing (as seen in Indexes) or correcting the specific query. Once the analysis is finished, the lines added in my.cnf are commented out and the service is restarted to return to normality. The diagnosis of the queries that appear, together with the rest of incidents, is in 9.13 (Troubleshooting con Pandora).

docs.title: Rebuilding the database
docs.text:
There is a point where optimizing stops being useful. When a table is so large that OPTIMIZE TABLE does not finish, gets stuck or demands free space there is not, the alternative is to rebuild. And it is worth understanding well what that means, because it is not an engine setting: it is a restore.

Rebuilding involves stopping the service, making a complete and consistent dump of the database, emptying it and loading the dump again. The effect is the same as that of an optimization taken to the extreme: the database is left compact and with fresh statistics. The price is a service stop that can last around an hour, plus the dump and reload time, which on large databases is measured in hours. That is why the rebuild is treated as a restore operation, with its backup, its window and its subsequent check, and not as a setting that is made on a Tuesday afternoon.

The decision criterion is simple: if the table fits in a maintenance window and there is space for the rebuild, it is optimized; if it does not fit, it is rebuilt. The complete procedure, with the partial rebuild of a database and the full rebuild, the service stop, the consistent dump and the reload, lives in 6.9 (Backup y restore). Here only the border between the two operations remains. If the rebuild comes preceded by a performance problem that is not understood, the general diagnosis is in 9.13 (Troubleshooting con Pandora).

docs.title: Manual partitioning of large tables
docs.text:
Spreading a huge table into smaller pieces has two advantages that are felt every day. The first, that a query by date range touches only the partition that corresponds to it, instead of walking the whole table. The second, that purging old data stops being a massive delete and becomes something much cheaper, because a whole partition can be discarded. On installations with a lot of volume, it is one of the most appreciated optimizations.

The prerequisite is the tablespace per table, that is, innodb_file_per_table enabled. Without it, partitioning makes no sense. The operation is done with an ALTER TABLE that declares the partitions by range on the timestamp of the data; the complete procedure and syntax are in 6.5 (Historical database). There is also the automatic partitioning of the historical database, which is the recommended path when the process does not need to be controlled by hand: it is configured from the Web console and it does not require writing SQL. Manual partitioning is for those who prefer that control or want to partition the active database, which the automatic one does not cover.

It is worth treating it, though, as an administration operation and not as a quick setting: it has to be planned with a maintenance window and a recent backup, and 6.5 holds the cost warnings that accompany the procedure. The schema on which it is applied and the specific table and column names are in 10.1 (Database schema) and 10.2 (Table reference).

docs.title: Quick reference and division of labour with other chapters
docs.text:
To close, the cheat sheet. First, the engine parameters and the value Pandora FMS applies, to have them at hand:

Parameter Value Parameter Value innodb_buffer_pool_size 25 % or 40 % of the RAM, depending on the system max_allowed_packet 64M innodb_lock_wait_timeout 90 innodb_file_per_table Enabled innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit 0 (in high availability, 2) innodb_flush_method O_DIRECT innodb_log_file_size 64M or 512M, depending on the system innodb_log_buffer_size 16M innodb_io_capacity 100, 300 or 1000, depending on the system thread_cache_size 8 or 32, depending on the system thread_stack 256K max_connections 100 or 300, depending on the system key_buffer_size 4M sql_mode Empty read_buffer_size 128K read_rnd_buffer_size 128K sort_buffer_size 1M join_buffer_size 4M

And the commands of this chapter, in a short list to copy:

# Locate the configuration file the engine applies
mysqld --help --verbose | head -40

# Measure the system load
vmstat 1 10

-- See the engine values hot
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb%';

-- Measure the fragmentation of the tables
SELECT ENGINE, TABLE_NAME,
       ROUND(DATA_LENGTH/1024/1024)  AS data_length,
       ROUND(INDEX_LENGTH/1024/1024) AS index_length,
       ROUND(DATA_FREE/1024/1024)    AS data_free,
       (DATA_FREE/(INDEX_LENGTH+DATA_LENGTH)) AS frag_ratio
  FROM information_schema.tables
 WHERE TABLE_TYPE = 'BASE TABLE'
   AND DATA_FREE > 0
 ORDER BY frag_ratio DESC;

-- Optimize the tables that need it and refresh the engine
OPTIMIZE TABLE <table>;
FLUSH TABLES;

-- Check the indexes of a table
SHOW INDEX FROM <table>;

The division with other chapters, so that you do not look where it is not:

Topic Chapter Historical database, retention, purging and automatic partitioning 6.5 (Historical database) Backup, restore and rebuild of the database 6.9 (Backup y restore) High availability, binary logs and their my.cnf 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)) Inventory of Web console options 9.2 (Full console configuration reference) Server configuration reference 9.3 (Full server configuration reference) General diagnosis and incidents 9.13 (Troubleshooting con Pandora) Sizing and capacity tools 9.14 (Análisis de volumetría y diseños para alta capacidad) Schema and table reference 10.1 (Database schema) and 10.2 (Table reference) Server and database frequently asked questions 12.2 (Servidor y base de datos) and 12.8 (Entornos grandes)

The idea that sums up the chapter is the one it opened with: Pandora FMS does not optimize the database for you. It gives you the diagnosis, the maintenance that purges and checks, and the documentation so that you keep it healthy. The rest is the administrator's craft: measure before touching, understand what each parameter does, do not trust a button that does not exist and know when the table is already too large to optimize it and it has to be rebuilt.

docs.title: Introduction: what a backup protects (and what it does not)
docs.text:
A backup goes unnoticed the day it is made. It is noticed the day it is needed. And that day never looks like the day it was scheduled: the server will not start, someone has deleted what they should not have, the disk has given up. This chapter is about making that day a bad time with a solution and not a permanent loss. What decides the difference is everything that is done beforehand: what gets copied, with which command and whether anyone ever tested that the backup can be restored.

What is at stake is everything the installation has accumulated: the metrics history, the events, the alerts and the configuration that sustains the monitoring. An accidental deletion, a disk that dies or an update gone wrong can sweep it away in a moment.

Before going into the matter, it is worth clearing up three confusions that claim whole installations.

High availability is not a backup. A high availability environment replicates the database hot so that the service does not go down, but it replicates the error too. If someone deletes a table on the master node, the deletion reaches the secondary node. Resynchronization between nodes in an HA environment uses a physical copy of the data, not a logical dump, and it is documented in 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)).

Migrating is not copying. Changing architecture, server or engine version is a move with its own procedures, and this chapter does not touch them: the migration to the new server architecture is in A3 (Compatibility and migration to the new server architecture) and the updates in 1.4 (Updates). This is about keeping what exists and returning it to its place.

And the third: a backup without a tested restore is a promise, not a safety net. A compressed file nobody has ever opened protects nothing. The only proof that a backup is worth anything is restoring it, even if it is on a test machine and with a toy database.

With that clear, this is what Pandora FMS offers and what it does not. It offers the scheduled console task, which dumps the main database as often as you schedule it; the DB Backup Manager, which administers those backups from the Web console; the full backup from the command line utility, which adds the files to the dump; and, of course, the manual commands of mysqldump and tar, which is where you always end up when something has to be done by hand.

What it does not offer, and it is worth knowing before trusting it: there is no automatic backup of the files (the scheduled task only dumps the main database) and no integrated backup of the historical database, which lives on another server and is copied separately, as explained in 6.5 (Historical database). The creation and scheduling of the task, with its parameters and its permissions, are documented in 2.5 (Console tasks). Here it is explained what that task produces, what it leaves out and how everything is restored.

The chapter follows the natural order of a real operation: first the inventory of what has to be copied, then each backup path (the manual dump, the scheduled task, the manager, the command line utility and the files) and, at the end, the restore and the rebuild of the database. The rebuild, which is the last resort when the engine no longer starts, is referenced from 6.8 (Database optimization): the criterion for when to rebuild instead of optimizing is there, and the procedures are here. The database encryption, which conditions what can be decrypted on restoring, is covered in 9.5 (Database encryption).

docs.title: What to back up in a Pandora FMS installation
docs.text:
A Pandora FMS installation is not a single thing. It is a database, some configuration files, the server programs, the Web console and, on every monitored machine, an EndPoint. The backup has to cover what cannot be rebuilt on its own:

Component Where it lives How it is copied Main database The MySQL engine, usually on the same machine as the console Dump with mysqldump (by hand) or the scheduled task Historical database Another MySQL server, if it is configured Its own dump: explained in 6.5 (Historical database) Server and EndPoints configuration /etc/pandora tar (The backup of the files) Server programs and plugins /usr/share/pandora_server tar Server data (remote configuration and collections) /var/spool/pandora/data_in tar Web console /var/www/html/pandora_console tar, or the full backup EndPoint Its installation directory (on Linux, /usr/share/pandora_agent) and its configuration (/etc/pandora) tar Tentacle /etc/tentacle tar

The database and the files go together. It is the rule that gets broken the most and the one that hurts the most. Restoring a database without the files leaves an installation that starts up halfway: the console opens, but the remote configuration of the EndPoints is not there, or the server plugins have disappeared. And the other way round: files without the database are a shell with no data. A truly complete backup has both halves.

Keep the backup off the server being copied. A backup that lives on the same disk as the original data protects you from an accidental deletion, but not from a disk failure, a fire or a rm with too much imagination. Take it out of the machine, to another server or to external storage, and do not leave it on the same file system.

Each piece is copied where it lives. In a distributed installation, with the database on one server, the console on another and the EndPoints spread out, there is no single machine from which to copy everything at once. The database is dumped where the engine is and the files of each server are packed on their server. The full backup in a single file, the one in the full backup from the command line, is only good when everything lives on the same machine.

Space and permissions

A dump takes up as much as the data it contains, and the files of a console with images and extensions can be quite large. Before launching a backup, check that the destination has more than enough free space: falling short halfway because the disk is full is the dumbest way to lose a backup. And save the files with restricted permissions: a database dump contains users, configuration and monitoring data that should not be accessible to just anyone.

docs.title: The database dump by hand
docs.text:
This is the basic tool, the one that works whenever the engine is running. The command is a mysqldump with the same two flags the product's scheduled task uses, and with placeholders so that you adapt it to your installation:

mysqldump '<database>' -h '<host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M | gzip > pandoradb.sql.gz

Each piece of the command has its reason:

  • <database>: the name of the database. In a fresh installation, it is pandora.
  • -h '<host>': the host of the engine. Use 127.0.0.1 if the database lives on the same machine, or its address if it is remote.
  • -u '<user>' and -p'<password>': the credentials to access the database. In a freshly made installation, the user is pandora. The -p goes attached to the password, with no space. If you leave it on its own, the client will prompt you for it and it will not be written in the terminal history.
  • --single-transaction: the dump is made inside a transaction, consistently, without blocking writes.
  • --max_allowed_packet=512M: the maximum packet size the client accepts when dumping. It is the value the scheduled task uses, and without it a large row or packet can abort the dump halfway.
  • | gzip > pandoradb.sql.gz: the dump is compressed on the fly. The resulting file is the one that is kept and the one that will be restored later.

There is no need to add flags for routines, triggers or events. The product schema defines none of the three, and the product's internal dumps do not use them. Adding them only adds noise to the command.

The historical database goes separately. If you have the historical database configured, it is not copied with this command. It lives on another server and needs its own dump, with the same flags and pointing at its host and its name. The detail of that database, its retention and its partitioning are in 6.5 (Historical database), and its backup is made with the same pattern:

mysqldump '<history_database>' -h '<history_host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M | gzip > pandoradb_history.sql.gz

With encryption on, the backup does not decrypt anything by itself

If the database uses column encryption, the backup carries the encrypted fields as they are and does not include the encryption passphrase, which is stored separately. Without that passphrase, there is nothing to decrypt on restoring and the encrypted data is left unreadable. The encryption procedure and where the passphrase lives are in 9.5 (Database encryption).

Do the services have to be stopped to copy? No. With --single-transaction the dump is consistent even if monitoring keeps writing, so stopping is not a requirement of the backup. Stopping is a matter of the restore and of the rebuild, which is when the order of operations does matter. To copy, it is enough that the engine is running and there is space at the destination.

Check the file when it finishes. A dump that is cut short halfway leaves a file that looks like a backup and is not one. Before accepting it as good, verify that the compressed file is complete:

gzip -t pandoradb.sql.gz

If the command returns nothing, the file is intact. And if the dump was cut short halfway, this is the time to repeat it, not three months from now.

docs.title: The scheduled backup from the console
docs.text:
Scheduling a backup so that you do not have to remember it is the most sensible thing you can do in this matter. The database backup task is created and scheduled in the Web console, in Discovery → Task list, on the Console tasks tab. Its creation, its parameters and its permissions are documented in 2.5 (Console tasks). Here it is time to explain what it leaves on the disk and what it does not.

What it produces. Each run creates two files in the configured path:

  • A compressed dump of the main database, with a name that carries the date.
  • A text summary of the same name, with the product version, the date and the PHP and MySQL versions of the server. It is the file you look at to know what each backup contains without opening it.

Both are left with 0600 permissions: only the user who created them can read them. The default path is the console's attachments folder, attachment/backups, and it can be changed to any directory with read and write permissions. The default retention is the last three backups of that task: when the number is exceeded, the oldest ones are deleted on their own.

When creating it, the task checks that mysqldump exists and that the connection to the database works, and validates that the save path exists and can be written to. If something fails, the task is not created. It is a check that avoids the classic backup that never ran because the path no longer existed.

What the task does not copy

The scheduled task dumps only the main database. It does not include the historical database (which is another database, on another server), nor the configuration files, nor the Web console, nor the EndPoints. Do not let anyone mistake it for a full backup. For that there is the utility of the full backup from the command line or the combination of the dump with the tar files of the backup of the files.

How it is restored. Just like a manual dump: the compressed file the task leaves is imported with gunzip -c … | mysql …, as explained in the restore. There is no automatic restore from the console: the restore is done by hand.

docs.title: The DB Backup Manager
docs.text:
The DB Backup Manager is the backup administration screen, in Admin tools → DB Backup Manager, and only the administrators of the Web console can enter it. It works on the same listing that the scheduled task feeds: the backups the task registers appear here, with the same folder and the same record.

At the top there is a filter by path of the backups, with the list of paths of the registered backups, and a search button to refresh the listing. Each backup shows its date, its size and a status:

  • OK: the file is in its place and can be downloaded and restored.
  • Lost: the record says it exists, but the file is not on the disk.
  • In Progress: there is a dump running at that moment.

With each OK backup there are three actions: download it to the local machine, delete it or restore it. The lost ones and those in progress can only be deleted. The manager's restore is not automatic: when you press the button, the console asks for confirmation and the restore is done by hand. The complete procedure, with the current syntax, is in the restore.

When there are lost backups, the Delete Lost button appears, which cleans all of those in that state at once.

A file deleted by hand does not disappear from the list

The manager does not walk the disk to build the listing: it trusts its record. If someone deletes a backup file outside the console, the backup does not disappear from the listing: it becomes lost, and it stays there until you use Delete Lost. It is the expected behaviour, and the reason the list can show backups that no longer exist.

docs.title: The full backup from the command line
docs.text:
So far, everything copied the database or the files separately. What remains is the only utility of the product that makes a full backup in a single step, and it does it from the command line: pandora_backup.sh. It is intended for installations where the server and the console share a machine, and it leaves a single compressed file with:

  • The dump of the database.
  • The complete Web console directory.
  • The configuration of /etc/pandora.
  • The server data of /var/spool/pandora/data_in.

The script is at /usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_backup.sh, it is run as root and it needs mysqldump available. With no parameter it shows its help, and these are its real options:

Option What it is for -c <path> Path of the Web console (for example, /var/www/html/pandora_console). From its configuration it takes the database credentials. -d <path> Directory where the backup file is left. -s <file> Backup file that is going to be restored. -f On restoring, it also restores the files, not only the database. -q Quiet mode, without messages. To launch it from cron. -b It does not copy or restore the database: only the files. -h Shows the help.

A backup is launched like this:

/usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_backup.sh -c /var/www/html/pandora_console -d /backup

The result is a pandorafms_backup_<date>.tar.gz file in the destination directory.

The restore is destructive

Restoring with -s merges nothing: the script deletes the current database and creates it again before importing the backup. With -f, it also overwrites the installation files. If the backup is old or half done, the result is worse than the problem you were going to solve. Before restoring, make sure you have a recent backup and that the file you pass is the right one:

/usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_backup.sh -c /var/www/html/pandora_console -s /backup/pandorafms_backup_2026-10-21-03-00-00.tar.gz -f

When to use it and when not to. It is the convenient option for a small server with everything on the same machine. In a distributed environment, with the database on one server, the console on another and the EndPoints spread out, it is no use. There, the dump of the database goes on one side and the tar files per component of the next section on the other.

docs.title: The backup of the files
docs.text:
The backup of the files is made with tar, component by component, with the real paths of the installation. The pattern is always the same:

tar -pcvzf pandora_configuration.tar.gz /etc/pandora
tar -pcvzf pandora_server.tar.gz /usr/share/pandora_server
tar -pcvzf pandora_console.tar.gz /var/www/html/pandora_console
tar -pcvzf pandora_data_in.tar.gz /var/spool/pandora/data_in
tar -pcvzf agent.tar.gz /usr/share/pandora_agent
tar -pcvzf tentacle.tar.gz /etc/tentacle

Each command packs and compresses (-z) one component, preserving permissions and owners (-p), which is what is needed for the restore to return the files exactly as they were. The Web console one preserves the images, the extensions and the customisations. The server data one includes the remote configuration of the EndPoints, the collections and the control files. On Linux EndPoints, the installation directory is /usr/share/pandora_agent. On other platforms it changes, and its configuration lives in /etc/pandora, which already goes in the first tar.

Three warnings so that the file backup does not fall short:

  • The server plugins can live outside /usr/share/pandora_server. If you have plugins or scripts of your own in other directories, add one tar for each.
  • The backup goes off the server. As with the dump: a tar that sleeps on the same disk does not protect you from a disk failure.
  • The server data carries more than it seems. Losing /var/spool/pandora/data_in is losing the configuration the EndPoints already had applied, and that is not recovered by reinstalling.

And the restore of these files, which is as simple as decompressing them in place, is covered in the restore.

docs.title: The restore
docs.text:
Restoring is not decompressing and hoping for the best. There is an order, and the order matters because each step writes in places the next one needs untouched.

1. Stop everything that writes. Stop the Pandora FMS server (systemctl stop pandora_server) and the local EndPoint if it is on the same machine (systemctl stop pandora_agent_daemon). The Web console must not be in use while the import runs. The Tentacle server can keep working: it will keep receiving data from the EndPoints and will process it when the server is back.

2. Restore the database. With the engine running, create the database if it does not exist:

CREATE DATABASE <database>;

And import the backup into it:

gunzip -c pandoradb.sql.gz | mysql -h '<host>' -u root -p <database>

The database name has to be the same

The backup was made on a database with a name, and restoring it on a different one forces you to adjust the configuration of the console and of the server afterwards. And if the database already has data, the import will replace it without warning: the dump drops and recreates every table. If you want to keep it, the alternative is in step 4.

3. Users and permissions. If the database user of the console and the server already exists and the restored database keeps its permissions, there is nothing to do. If you have created a new database, give the user access to it. And if the user has been lost (for example, after rebuilding the data directory of the engine), recreate it with the same syntax the product installers apply. It is the syntax current in MySQL 8:

CREATE USER '<user>'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
ALTER USER '<user>'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH caching_sha2_password BY '<password>';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <database>.* TO '<user>'@'%';

The old single-statement form, GRANT … IDENTIFIED BY …, is retired in MySQL 8 and fails: if you see it in an old recipe, replace it with these three.

4. Recommended alternative: the path that does not overwrite. If the current database has data you want to keep, do not import over it as in step 2. The steps, in short:

  1. Create the new database and give permissions to the console user:

    CREATE DATABASE <new_database>;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <new_database>.* TO '<user>'@'%';

  2. Import the backup into it:

    gunzip -c pandoradb.sql.gz | mysql -h '<host>' -u root -p <new_database>

  3. Point the console to the new database: in include/config.php of the Web console, change $config["dbname"]="<database>"; to $config["dbname"]="<new_database>";.

  4. Point the server: in /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf, change dbname <database> to dbname <new_database>.
  5. Restart the server and log in to the console again.

5. Restore the files. Each tar is decompressed in place with -C /, because the paths inside the file are absolute:

tar -xzf pandora_configuration.tar.gz -C /
tar -xzf pandora_server.tar.gz -C /
tar -xzf pandora_console.tar.gz -C /
tar -xzf pandora_data_in.tar.gz -C /

Doing it as root, permissions and owners are returned exactly as they were. If the console is left with the wrong owner, the web server will not be able to write in its folders and you will notice as soon as you try to upload an image.

6. The "reinstall and restore" case. When the original machine no longer exists, the order is the other way round: first a clean installation is made, with the same version, following 1.1 (Installation). Then the restore goes on top: the database and the files. This is not a migration (that one is in A3): it is putting back in place what was there.

7. Check. A restore does not end when the last command ends, but when everything works again:

  • The Web console opens and shows the agents, the modules and the data from before.
  • The server starts and processes: systemctl start pandora_server and a look at its log.
  • The console cron is still in place: the entry in /etc/crontab that calls the console cron every minute is the one that drives events, alerts and maintenance.
  • The EndPoints report again. If any of them does not, its local configuration or its access key did not come back well.

And start in order: first the engine (already running), then the server and finally the EndPoints.

docs.title: Rebuilding the database
docs.text:
The rebuild is the last resort, and it is a restore, not a tune-up. 6.8 (Database optimization) explains when it is due: when optimizing a table no longer finishes, when the engine does not start after a configuration change or when the database needs to be rebuilt from scratch. Here are the procedures.

Partial rebuild. It is about returning a database to a compact and healthy state, with the service stopped. The process: stop the server and leave the Web console out of use; then dump the database, delete it, recreate it and import the dump.

systemctl stop pandora_server
mysqldump '<database>' -h '<host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M | gzip > /tmp/pandoradb.sql.gz

Then, in the MySQL client:

DROP DATABASE <database>;
CREATE DATABASE <database>;

And the import and the start:

gunzip -c /tmp/pandoradb.sql.gz | mysql -h '<host>' -u root -p <database>
systemctl start pandora_server

The dump can take minutes or hours, depending on the size. The import takes just as long. It is a maintenance window operation, not something for a spare moment between tasks. In a large installation, the service stop alone is planned around an hour, and to that the dump and the reload are added. The process can be automated, but for its delicate nature it is better done by hand, with the window reserved and a recent backup already made.

Full rebuild. When the engine does not start or the data directory has to be rebuilt (for example, after a change in my.cnf that prevents it from starting), the rebuild goes one step further. It rebuilds the data directory of the engine. First, if the engine does not start, return to the previous configuration so that it can come up, and take the chance to get the dump out:

mysqldump '<database>' -h '<host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M | gzip > /home/pandora/pandoradb.sql.gz

With the backup safe, and with the Pandora FMS server stopped (as in the partial rebuild), stop the engine and rebuild its data directory:

systemctl stop mysql
mv /var/lib/mysql /var/lib/mysql.bak
mkdir /var/lib/mysql
mysqld --initialize --datadir /var/lib/mysql

mysqld --initialize generates a temporary password for the root user. Write it down, because you are going to need it in the next step. Then adjust permissions and start:

chown -R mysql:mysql /var/lib/mysql
chcon -R system_u:object_r:mysqld_db_t:s0 /var/lib/mysql
systemctl start mysql

The chcon command is for systems with SELinux (the RHEL family). On Ubuntu it is not needed. And in the distributions of the RHEL family, the service is called mysqld instead of mysql.

Enter with the temporary password, change it and get the database ready:

ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
CREATE DATABASE <database>;

Import the dump and recreate the database user used by the console and the server with the current syntax (the same as in the restore):

gunzip -c /home/pandora/pandoradb.sql.gz | mysql -u root -p <database>

CREATE USER '<user>'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
ALTER USER '<user>'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH caching_sha2_password BY '<password>';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <database>.* TO '<user>'@'%';

There are no binary logs to delete anymore

The old full rebuild recipes deleted by hand the binary log files of the data directory. That step no longer applies: on a single server, the standard Pandora FMS installers and deployments disable the binary logs (skip-log-bin); if you set up the engine by hand, confirm the line is in my.cnf. In a high availability environment the binary logs are mandatory, but there the rebuild is another story and it is covered in 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)).

Finally, check that the engine is running with the parameters you expect, that the Web console and the server connect to the database and that everything works. The variables query confirms that the applied configuration is what you think it is:

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb%';

When you have it confirmed, delete the old directory:

rm -rf /var/lib/mysql.bak

If this is a high availability server, the services are different (pandora_ha instead of pandora_server), and the start, the stop and the resynchronization of an HA environment are documented in 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)).

docs.title: Quick reference and division of labour with other chapters
docs.text:
To close, the cheat sheet. The commands of the chapter, in a table to copy:

For Command Dump the main database mysqldump '<database>' -h '<host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M|gzip > pandoradb.sql.gz Dump the historical database mysqldump '<history_database>' -h '<history_host>' -u '<user>' -p'<password>' --single-transaction --max_allowed_packet=512M|gzip > pandoradb_history.sql.gz Restore a dump gunzip -c pandoradb.sql.gz|mysql -h '<host>' -u root -p <database> Check that a dump is complete gzip -t pandoradb.sql.gz Full backup (database and files) /usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_backup.sh -c /var/www/html/pandora_console -d /backup Restore with the full backup /usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_backup.sh -c /var/www/html/pandora_console -s <file> -f Copy a component tar -pcvzf <file>.tar.gz <path>

And the division with other chapters, so you do not look in the wrong place:

Topic Chapter Create and schedule the backup task, with its parameters and permissions 2.5 (Console tasks) Historical database, its retention and its partitioning 6.5 (Historical database) When to rebuild instead of optimizing 6.8 (Database optimization) High availability and its resynchronization between nodes 6.10 (Alta Disponibilidad (HA)) Database encryption and encryption passphrase 9.5 (Database encryption) Installation and reinstallation 1.1 (Installation) Updates 1.4 (Updates) Migration to the new server architecture A3 (Compatibility and migration to the new server architecture)

And the idea that sums up the chapter, the same one it opened with: a backup is only worth anything if it has been restored at least once. Schedule it, keep it off the server and, from time to time, restore it in a test environment. The day it is really needed, there will be no time to find out it did not work.

docs.title: Secure configuration
docs.text:
Pandora FMS is installed with a few security decisions already made, but leaving it "ready for production" is another matter. This chapter gathers what has to be touched so that an installation survives an audit: what is exposed, how it is encrypted, what is hardened in the base system and what is enabled on the platform itself.

The underlying idea is simple: the less you expose and the more you log, the less you will have to fix later. Everything that follows is concrete measures, not theory.

docs.title: Exposed surface
docs.text:
The first thing is to know what listens. And here there is a detail that surprises anyone coming from other tools: the Pandora FMS server does not listen on any port. The one that listens is the Tentacle server, which receives data from the EndPoints; the Pandora FMS server only reads the files Tentacle leaves on disk. And the EndPoint does not listen either: it is the one that starts the connection to the server.

The ports that matter:

Component Port Is it published? Web console 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) Yes, 443; 80 only if you redirect API Console HTTP/HTTPS Only if you use it from outside Tentacle 41121/TCP Only towards the machines that report Tentacle RMM 41123/TCP Only if you use RMM over Tentacle Database (MySQL) 3306/TCP No, unless it is remote by design SNMP trap console 162/UDP Only from the devices that send traps

The practical rule: expose only what is essential and leave the rest listening on 127.0.0.1. If the database only serves the machine itself, there is no point in it being reachable from the network, and that is fixed in a minute (see the MySQL hardening below).

docs.title: Accounts and credentials
docs.text:
• Named users. Each person, their own account. No shared accounts: if you do not know who did what, the audit log is useless.
  • No excess privileges. Each user with the profile they need and nothing more. Group permissions and advanced ACL fit here.
  • Double authentication on accounts with console access, and especially on administrators.
  • Application users without remote access. If you create users to run services, disable their shell so they cannot log in over SSH.
  • The superuser, with sudo. For anything that requires privileges, sudo, not an open root session.
  • Complex database passwords, and not the factory ones. The MySQL password is the key to everything else.
  • Sensitive data encrypted. The credentials the product stores (credential store, module passwords) can be encrypted in the database (see below).

docs.title: Encryption and transport
docs.text:
Everything that travels over the network should be encrypted, and Pandora FMS allows it at every leg:

  • Web console over HTTPS. The console supports HTTPS with a web server certificate, and there is a setting to force everyone to use HTTPS.
  • Session cookies over SSL only. In sensitive environments, in php.ini: 
    session.cookie_httponly = 1
session.cookie_secure = 1
    Note: with this, the console stops working over HTTP. That is exactly the point, but you need to know it before enabling it.
  • Database over TLS. The connection between the server (and the console) and MySQL can be encrypted with SSL/TLS.
  • Tentacle with SSL/TLS. Tentacle has four levels: no encryption (default), basic SSL/TLS, SSL/TLS with a certificate at both ends and SSL/TLS with CA validation, which is the recommended one.

docs.title: Password encryption
docs.text:
Pandora FMS can encrypt the passwords stored in the database. The key is generated from a passphrase you provide, and it is not stored in the database: passwords cannot be recovered from a dump.

The passphrase is set in two places, encryption_passphrase, both in /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf and in the console's config.php, and then the encryption script is run:

/usr/bin/pandora_encrypt_db /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf

If you lose the passphrase, you lose the passwords

The encryption passphrase cannot be recovered. Keep it in a safe place or back up config.php and pandora_server.conf. To decrypt (for example, before changing the passphrase), use the same script with -d.

docs.title: Base system hardening
docs.text:
The product is as secure as the machine that hosts it. These are the minimums expected from the operating system:

  • System up to date. Update before going into production, and then periodically. Pandora FMS's package inventory helps you locate vulnerable versions.
  • Access audit active. The system security log (/var/log/secure) must be active and monitored.
  • SSH hardened. It is the most critical point of any Linux server. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config: change the default port, set PermitRootLogin no, disable AllowTcpForwarding and PermitTunnel, review (and delete if unnecessary) root's remote access keys, and set a warning with Banner.
  • MySQL local only. If the database is internal, make it listen only on 127.0.0.1 with bind-address = 127.0.0.1 in [mysqld] of /etc/my.cnf. Check with netstat that it is not still listening on 0.0.0.0.
  • Apache not giving away its version. Add ServerTokens Prod so the headers do not reveal the web server version.
  • Fewer services. Check with netstat -tulpn (and lsof) what is listening and why. What you do not need, out; what listens on 0.0.0.0 for no reason, to localhost.
  • Synchronized time. NTP on the server. Besides the logs, double authentication depends on the time matching.

docs.title: Secure configuration of the console and the server
docs.text:
Once in the platform itself, what is worth tying down:

  • Force HTTPS in the console.
  • Protected API: a list of allowed IP addresses and a strong password for the API. The * wildcard leaves the API open to anyone: do not use it in production.
  • Advanced ACL to restrict which sections each profile sees.
  • Audit log enabled and exported (see the next section).
  • Read-only mode on the most sensitive EndPoints: if they do not need remote configuration changes, they should not accept them.
  • Limit who uploads executables (plugins, collections) with the corresponding permissions.
  • Permissions of the server configuration file. Check that pandora_server.conf is not readable by everyone.
  • Change the administrator password after the first start. Do not leave the administration account with the first-boot password.

docs.title: Enabling 2FA
docs.text:
Double authentication is the measure with the best effort-to-result ratio: even if someone steals your password, without the second factor they do not get in. It is enabled in the global authentication configuration (Double authentication) and each user turns it on in Operation → Workspace → Edit my user. Force 2FA for all users makes it mandatory for everyone.

It needs a code-generating app on the user's phone and the server and the phone to have synchronized time. To disable it for a specific user without going through the console, there is the CLI (--disable_double_auth). The details of the fields are in Part 04 · External authentication.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
Pandora FMS keeps an audit log with the important changes and actions in the console: which user, which action, when and a description. It is queried in Management → Admin tools → System audit log, with filters by action, user, IP address, text and time range, and it can be exported to CSV.

It comes disabled

The audit log is not active by default. It is enabled in Management → Settings → System Settings → General setup → Security, with the Enable audit log option, and saved. A log that is not turned on does not audit anything.

What is truly useful is not looking at it by hand, but centralizing it in an external system in real time, so that a local administrator cannot erase their tracks. The clean way is Rsyslog, which already comes installed with the server:

  • In the console, the log is written to /var/www/html/pandora_console/log/audit.log.
  • An Rsyslog imfile tails that file and forwards it over TCP to an external receiver. A dedicated ruleset is used to send only the audit and not the whole system journal.
  • On the receiver, another ruleset stores the lines in its own file.

The technical annex on centralizing the audit log with Rsyslog has the full configuration, end to end, with the sender and the receiver. With that, the trail leaves the machine in seconds and stays where no one inside can touch it.

docs.title: Password policy
docs.text:
Enterprise installations have a password policy in Configuration → Password policy. It is what turns "set a password" into "set a password that holds up". Among other things, it controls:

Setting What it does Enable password policy Activates the whole mechanism Minimum length How many characters at least Password expiration Days of validity; 0 = never expires Must have numbers and symbols Requires character types History and compare with the previous one Prevents reusing passwords Apply to administrators The policy also applies to them Force change on first start Forces a change on first login (generates a new token for the API) User locked if login fails Duration of the temporary lockout Number of failed attempts How many failures are allowed (minimum two) Maximum temporary lockouts With 0, there is never a permanent lockout; with a number, the user is permanently locked until unlocked Password reset and excluded words Enables "I forgot my password" and blocks specific words

docs.title: Account lockout and unlock
docs.text:
With the policy active, a user who accumulates failures is locked, and if they exceed the maximum number of temporary lockouts, permanently locked. In both cases an administrator unlocks them from the user record, in the Users section (not from "Edit my user").

And since version 805, also from the CLI:

pandora_manage /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf --unlock_user <user>

That command is the safety net for the awkward case: the locked user is the administrator.
